MN202611_1gyhtj6aq00.t:
Historic space mission lifts off with first Pakistan astronaut aboard Chinese rocket

China launched its Shenzhou-24 space mission on Wednesday carrying three astronauts to its Tiangong space station, including Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to join a Chinese crewed space mission.

Beijing said it hopes the flight will strengthen ties with Islamabad, as the two countries mark 75 years of co-operation in space.

Speaking to reporters at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, Ali said he was "carrying the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis".

The mission, which also comprises of commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi, took off at 08:18 (00:18 GMT) from the Gobi desert. Minutes later, it was declared a "complete success".

While in space, the Shenzhou-24 crew will carry out experiments and test technology in fields like aerospace medicine, combustion and study the affects of space on living organisms.

The mission comprises of payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, flight engineer Wu Yi and commander Tang Hongbo

They will also study how the space environment affects aging, with the hope of developing new ways to prevent and treat age-related vascular diseases.

Ali will conduct studies on photosynthesis in bacteria and the effects of radiation and microgravity - a very weak gravity in space - on seeds.

The former fighter pilot will return to Earth after a short stay, with two other Chinese crew members who have been at the space station since May.

Tang and Wu will spend six months at Tiangong space station along with Zhu Yangzhu, a member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, which lifted off in May this year. Zhu has been studying how the human body adapts to long periods in space.

The Shenzhou-24 is also a diplomatic moment for Beijing.

China has poured billions of dollars into its space programme and its prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.

It is now keen to show the world that the station has the potential to become an international research platform rather than an exclusive Chinese facility.

Hundreds of people gathered at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center before dawn waving Chinese and Pakistani flags.

This also comes at a time when Beijing is trying to establish itself as a major alternative to the US-led space programme, with a bold goal to land Chinese astronauts on the moon for the first time by 2030.

For Pakistan, which does not have its own spacecraft to send astronauts to space, being invited to be a part of this mission is significant.

Ali and Khurram Dawood, the other candidate to reach the final stage in the Shenzhou-24 crew selection, were trained in China and had worked in Chinese space stations under the supervision of Chinese experts.

Mastering Chinese language was one of his "biggest challenges", Ali said, according to Pakistani media.

MN202611_1xazuodrs2z.t:
Mauricio Pochettino has taken over a Manchester United team in the Premier League relegation zone

Last season, Tottenham - a member of the so-called 'big six' - escaped relegation from the Premier League on the final day.

Now, with Manchester United making their worst start to a league season since 1972, it begs the question: are United this season's Spurs?

Well while Tottenham finished 17th with just 41 points, they actually started the season better than United have. After 11 games last season, Spurs were riding high in fifth with 18 points - 10 more than United have now.

But one of the biggest myths in football is 'the table never lies' and it was certainly lying about Tottenham at this stage last season.

While the table was prompting talk of a possible Champions League place, expected goals (xG) had already recognised a relegation battle lay ahead for Tottenham, even predicting the position they'd finish in.

United's expected goal difference is almost identical to Tottenham's at this stage last season, but this time the table is more honest, even if United are perhaps not as bad as it makes out.

But there's no denying United's statistics are those of a team in a relegation battle, with many of them in the bottom six of Premier League teams this season.

While United have performed poorly defensively, their attack is actually not bad.

Remarkably, United have taken the most shots in the Premier League so far this season, and their expected goals scored figure is in the top five.

But what new head coach Mauricio Pochettino has to implement quickly is some quality control when it comes to shots at both ends of the pitch. United are converting just 7% of their chances and conceding 16% of their opponents' - a poor combination for any team.

And it's not simply down to finishing or shot-stopping, though they should have scored a few more. Based on xG per shot, United are currently taking the second-worst chances to score and giving up the easiest ones at the back.

As a result, Opta give United just over a one-in-four chance of being relegated at the end of the season (27.5%), making them the fifth-most likely side to go down after Crystal Palace, Sunderland, Ipswich and Coventry.

By analysing historical and team performances as well as the strength of opponents, Opta predict the % chance of each club finishing in each position in the League.

While the above means it's more likely United will survive, it's worth noting the one position Opta predicts United are most likely to finish is 18th, with a 10.1% chance. That would mean the 13-time Premier League winners are relegated.

There's a 90% chance they finish anywhere else, but the next most likely are the three places just above the relegation zone, including a 9.9% chance of them finishing where Tottenham did last season.

History also suggests a relegation battle lies ahead for United given their poor start.

Of the 26 previous sides that had exactly eight points after 11 games, 13 survived and 13 were relegated. Among those that stayed up, only four finished more than six points above the danger zone.

A top-half finish looks unlikely. Since the competition became a 20-team league in 1995-96, no side has ever finished in the top half after taking eight points or fewer from their first 11 games.

Two teams did finish there more than 30 years ago but they had four more games to climb the table as teams played 42 games a season in those days.

Having said that, both were in the top half at the 38-game mark so United finishing there wouldn't be entirely unprecedented.

It's a big ask, though, as the club have already taken 19 points fewer from the fixtures they've played than they did last season.

Even if they were to repeat the results that led to them finishing third from now on, they would still only reach 52 points, the number Chelsea narrowly finished 10th with last season

Though United are without a win in nine Premier League matches, their remaining fixtures of 2026 do offer some hope.

While they have a tough home game against Brentford this weekend and a trip to champions Arsenal just before Christmas, their other five games are against teams currently in the bottom seven - sides we must, at this point, call relegation rivals

So despite suffering the worst first game by a Manchester United manager for 100 years in the 4-0 defeat at Liverpool , Pochettino will hope to quickly quash any concerns his new club will be embroiled in the same fight as his former one last season.

MN202611_72gtd89pu2.t:
The waste was dumped over garden fences in South Wigston over several months

Two fly-tippers were able to dump huge amounts of household waste over their garden fences without being detected for several months, with the pile eventually reaching 20 tonnes.

It was spotted on land owned by a business in South Wigston, Leicestershire, earlier in the year.

However, due to the location of the fly-tip, it was not immediately visible to employees of the business, which Oadby and Wigston Borough Council said "allowed the offenders to act over several months".

The two individuals responsible were each issued with a £600 fixed penalty notice following an interview under caution, the authority added, while a third person was cautioned for their role in the offence.

Before the rubbish could be cleared, the council's environmental health officers worked with the business to gather evidence to prove who had been responsible.

The authority has not specified which business was affected by the fly-tipping, or from where the rubbish was sourced.

The waste was reported to Oadby and Wigston Borough Council

The council said it had also recently issued another £600 fine after a resident's waste was found in a lay-by off Gartree Road in Oadby.

They had not fly-tipped the rubbish themselves, the authority added, but had paid a rogue operator in good faith to take it away.

According to the council, residents have a duty of care for their waste until it is disposed of correctly and should ensure it is given to a licensed waste operator.

Councillor Samina Haq, leader of the council, said: "There is simply no excuse for fly-tipping. It damages our environment, costs money to clear up and is unfair on the overwhelming majority of residents and businesses who dispose of their waste responsibly.

"These successful cases send a clear message that we will investigate reports, gather evidence and take action against those responsible.

"Please continue to report fly-tipping whenever you see it and, if you pay someone to remove your waste, always make sure they are properly licensed."

MN202611_300hsrxg8p.t:
The Hera spacecraft will study the 150m-wide (490ft) asteroid called Dimorphos

A spacecraft has arrived at an asteroid to investigate the damage caused by an unprecedented cosmic crash.

It what may sound like the plot of a disaster movie, Nasa's Dart spacecraft deliberately smashed into the space rock in 2022 to knock it off course.

The Nasa craft was obliterated on impact. Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) mission, called Hera, is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision - with the first images set to be released later on Wednesday.

The asteroid poses no threat, instead this was the first ever test of our planetary defences to see what action we could take if a space rock was heading for our planet.

"Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission.

This was the last image from Dart before it crashed into Dimorphos in 2022

The crash test focussed on a pair of asteroids: a larger one called Didymos - about 730m (2,400ft) wide - which is orbited by a smaller rock called Dimorphos, about 150m (490ft) wide.

The Dart spacecraft targeted Dimorphos, hurtling into the rock at 22,000km per hour (14,000mph). Images beamed back showed the asteroid's rocky surface coming ever closer until the feed cut out on impact.

It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 10,000km long (6,200 miles), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.

The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.

Before the collision it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the Dart crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.

But the arrival of the second spacecraft, Hera, will help scientists to answer many more questions.

"Dart exploded in the asteroid, and therefore we don't have the information of what is its final state," explained Michel.

"The impact could have left a crater - and if it is the case, we need to understand the size and the depth. Or [the impact] may have entirely reshaped the asteroid."

A 10,000km-long (6,200 miles) debris trail was spotted by the Hubble Space Telescope

The Hera mission will spend the next year studying Dimorphos, and take a look at Didymos too.

The spacecraft is packed with instruments, and it also has two small shoe-boxed sized satellites onboard, which can study the impact site up close, and then later land on the asteroid.

A key task is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was.

This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth.

"It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team.

"We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'."

Hera has already sent back an image of Didymos with Dimorphos in the background

Asteroids pose a significant threat to our planet.

The biggest, which measure more than a kilometre across, could cause global devastation. But medium-sized asteroids around the same dimensions as Dimorphos could wipe out a city.

"We all know what happened to the dinosaurs, right? And we don't want that to happen to us," said Carolyn Ernst, Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, who works on both the Dart and Hera missions.

"The good news for us is that there are far fewer potential threats out there in the Solar System than there were millions of years ago. But there are objects out there."

She said the biggest asteroids have been spotted, and none are heading to Earth.

"The smallest stuff isn't too much of a threat because our atmosphere protects us," she added.

"But there's a size range in the middle where we don't know where all of them are, and it could, if impacted, cause problems for humanity. And if we can find out about that and know about that, well, we sure as heck would want to try to stop that."

Hera has two small satellites onboard to study the asteroid up close

Scientists want to gather as much intelligence as they can about space rocks - to make us as well equipped as possible to deal with whatever the Universe throws at us.

A new mission is launching in 2027 to track potentially hazardous asteroids: a space telescope called the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor.

There are also more visits planned to asteroids, including to one called Apophis, which is about 450m (1,480ft) long.

Apophis was discovered in 2004 and it was initially thought it might hit the Earth as early as 13 April 2029.

But now scientists understand its orbit better, and say it won't hit us for at least the next 100 years. Instead of a crash in 2029, it will fly just 32,000km (20,000 miles) above our surface.

This will give scientists the rare chance to study a space rock up-close.

Two spacecraft will head to Apophis, including Nasa's Osiris-Apex (which previously grabbed a sample from another asteroid called Bennu) and Ramses, a joint mission between ESA and the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA).

MN202611_7zsuyjlrfd.t:
President Cyril Ramaphosa has faced calls to resign over his handling of the "Farmgate" scandal

A South African court is due to rule on President Cyril Ramaphosa's attempt to overturn a report that found he has a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm.

In 2022, an independent panel said Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct relating to the theft of $580,000 (£443,000), hidden in a sofa, at his Phala Phala game farm in the Limpopo province. He denied any wrongdoing.

Ramaphosa challenged the findings of the report after the Constitutional Court ruled that parliament had violated the constitution by blocking moves to impeach him.

The ruling could either exonerate the president or clear the way for him to possibly face impeachment.

Wednesday's ruling will be handed down by the Western Cape high court - the same court that blocked a parliamentary committee from proceeding with the impeachment process while a review challenge of the report is under way.

The scandal, dubbed "Farmgate" by local media, has has dogged Ramaphosa since it emerged in 2022, when former spy chief Arthur Fraser reported the matter to police in a dossier.

Fraser, an ally of former President Jacob Zuma, accused Ramaphosa of concealing the theft from the police and tax authorities.

The break-in happened in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.

Earlier this month, two people were found guilty of the theft.

Ramaphosa confirmed that a robbery had taken place but said the money had been from the legitimate sale of buffalo from his livestock business.

Several investigations cleared him of any wrongdoing, but parliament began an impeachment proceedings in 2022 and appointed an independent panel to investigate the allegations.

The panel made a series of damaging findings, including that there was "substantial doubt about the legitimacy of the source of the currency that was stolen".

It also concluded that Ramaphosa "has a case to answer".

Ramaphosa initially challenged the report in court but withdrew his application after parliament voted against adopting its findings.

He revived the legal challenge again in May this year after the Constitutional Court, the country's highest court , ruled that parliament had acted unconstitutionally by blocking moves to impeach him.

It ordered parliament to refer the report to an impeachment committee.

In his latest challenge, Ramaphosa argued that the panel had "misconceived its mandate, misjudged the information placed before it and misinterpreted the four charges advanced against me".

If the Western Cape High Court rules in his favour, it could bring the current impeachment process to an end, unless parliament successfully challenges the decision.

A ruling against him would allow the parliamentary committee to examine the charges against the president and make a recommendation.

If it recommends impeachment, the matter is put to a vote. A two-thirds majority in parliament is required to remove the president.

Ramaphosa's ANC has enough votes to block this.

Ramaphosa is the first president to face impeachment proceedings under new rules introduced in 2018.

MN202611_1vy4lkkxi1e.t:
Hunter Schafer first came across Blade Runner when the 2017 sequel was released

"What does it mean to be human?" is a question that's always been at the heart of Blade Runner.

The first film in the series, released in 1982, depicted a technologically advanced yet dystopian version of Los Angeles in the then-distant future of 2019.

While the movie's flying cars haven't - quite - materialised yet in the real world, Blade Runner's themes of technological progress and the threats it poses feel just as relevant.

At least that's what the cast and crew of Blade Runner 2099, a new TV series set in the same universe, are hoping.

BBC Newsbeat spoke to stars Hunter Schafer, Lewis Gribben and Dimitri Abold, plus showrunner Silka Luisa, to ask why they think themes of artificial consciousness and existential threats still resonate.

The original Blade Runner, directed by Sir Ridley Scott, is considered a sci-fi classic that had a long-lasting influence on the genre.

It told the story of Detective Deckard, played by Harrison Ford, who hunted down synthetic humans known as replicants.

Schafer says her first exposure to the series was actually marketing for Blade Runner 2049 - the film sequel starring Ford and Ryan Gosling in 2017.

"I never thought I'd have the opportunity to make an addition to the world," she says.

"And so when that opportunity came along, I was quite thrilled."

Blade Runner 2099 is set 80 years after the original film, and portrays a Los Angeles where replicants have taken over.

Schafer plays Cora, a fugitive human forced to team up with replicant Olwen (played by Michelle Yeoh), as she tries to track down an artefact that could save humanity.

Schafer stars alongside Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh in the new TV adaptation

The series lands at a time when there are disagreements about the nature of the threat AI could pose to humans .

"I think it's particularly relevant right now, especially for the youth and young people who are inheriting a world that's asking a lot of the same questions that the show asks," says Schafer.

"I think that's timely and hopefully helpful to some degree."

But Blade Runner 2099 isn't "necessarily about just AI", says showrunner Luisa.

"It's this bigger question of what is the world going to be in 15 years and how can you plan for it?" she says.

The first Blade Runner also touched on themes of corporate greed and environmental damage, which are evident in the new series.

Luisa hopes the theme of a future that "is not going to be what you were promised" resonates with viewers today.

"The idea that you were born into a world and you thought you were expecting certain aspects of your life just to roll out," she says.

"That system is collapsing. And so what will be your place in whatever comes next?"

Blade Runner 2049 won awards and scored well with reviewers, but reports suggested it didn't hit box office targets.

This was partly blamed on marketing for the film trying to appeal more to existing fans than new ones - so what would the cast say to get younger viewers on board?

"It's just a very rich world," says Gribben, who plays Cora's younger brother Elias.

Gribben also points out that Blade Runner 2099, which employed "hundreds of artists and craftspeople" according to its makers, is a celebration of traditional film-making despite its themes.

"I think a lot of people crave human stories," he says.

"They crave new kind of worlds and new things.

"And I think studios will rely more on technology to make better-looking movies, but they won't have that soul."

Abold, who plays Cora's human ally Bebeto, says one of the show's key messages is about "the connections that you make".

"And the connections that you make are the foundation of humanity," he says.

"Because at the end of the day, all we have is ourselves and each other, right? And that's what feeds any human emotional experience."

Cora is helped by human allies including her brother Elias (Lewis Gribben) and Bebeto (Dimitri Abold)

Reviews for Blade Runner 2099 have been mostly positive, with a score of 72% on Rotten Tomatoes , external and an average of 65% on review aggregator Metacritic , external .

There was praise for the lead performances, the show's visual style and the way it updates the themes established in previous series entries.

The most common criticism was the show's pacing, with several critics describing it as a slow-burn and questioning whether Blade Runner worked as well off the big screen.

Schafer says she felt a lot of pressure when she signed up for the show,

"It's something that we were all aware of when making this show," she says.

"Everybody who was working on this show loves Blade Runner.

"Most people who love film-making love Blade Runner, everybody brought their best to work.

Blade Runner 2099 is available on Prime Video from 25 November.

MN202611_xurba2k7qw.t:
Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe

A Zimbabwean court has issued an arrest warrant for Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe, the youngest son of the country's late former president Robert Mugabe, after he failed to appear in court.

Mugabe was arrested earlier this month alongside four others over assault allegations on a police officer during an investigation into the suspected smuggling of luxury vehicles.

The group subsequently faced charges of robbery and malicious damage to property. They have yet to enter pleas.

They were granted bail on 6 November and were due back in court on Tuesday. However, Mugabe failed to attend. His co-accused, an aide and three security guards appeared and were remanded until 10 December.

Prosecutors allege that Mugabe and the others assaulted an investigating officer using their hands and broomsticks.

The officer's phone was allegedly taken and smashed on the ground, while one of the accused is said to have seized the officer's loaded pistol.

Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe.

Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for 37 years before being forced from power in 2017, aged 93, following a military intervention. He died in 2019.

His son has attracted public attention in recent years over a series of legal troubles and his high-profile lifestyle.

Last month, he admitted to drug-related charges involving the possession of cannabis.

In April, he was deported from neighbouring South Africa after pleading guilty to pointing a firearm and being in the country illegally. He had been arrested following the shooting of a 23-year-old man at his home.

In 2023, he was arrested in Harare, Zimbabwe's capital, over allegations that he damaged property and spat at a police officer during a party.

He was later freed after reaching an out-of-court settlement with the complainant, who was a friend.

MN202611_1mj7xdtzusf.t:
Bayern initially aim to find young players from Bavaria before looking further afield

Bayern Munich are one of the elite powers in European football and current home of Ballon d'Or winner and England captain Harry Kane.

But, while Kane is the latest hugely successful foreign import at Bayern, the German giants also put a particular focus on producing their own elite young talent.

In 2013, Bayern had four homegrown players in the starting line-up as they won the Champions League.

Repeating that victory, and continuing the club's history of nurturing young players, is what director of youth development and campus Jochen Sauer says Bayern are aiming for.

Sauer joined from RB Salzburg in 2017 when the academy campus opened in another part of Munich, away from the first-team training complex.

The club's motto "Mia San Mia" translates to "we are who we are" and Sauer says it has always been the club's goal to have a local homegrown element in its senior side.

"It was always our identity and philosophy to be a regional club, but at the same time to be competitive internationally and on Champions League level," Sauer tells BBC Sport. "But always having a core of our team coming from the Munich area and the Bavarian region with a deep identification with the club and the city.

"Our recruitment guidelines, especially for the under-11 to the under-15 teams, is trying to recruit as much talent as possible from the Munich area and the region of Bavaria."

Munich-born Croatia international Josip Stanisic is a good example. The midfielder, 26, signed as an under-17 player from local outfit SC Furstenfeldbruck, while 22-year-old Aleksandar Pavlovic joined the academy aged eight and has worked his way up to the first team and is a Germany international.

But perhaps the biggest name to come out of the academy in recent times is Jamal Musiala. The former Chelsea youth player, who joined aged 16, is a star for Bayern and Germany and has already won six Bundesliga titles at just 23 years old.

It was part of the club's strategy to bring in the best young foreign players, and those with German passports, to the club, but they also enjoyed a bit of luck.

The move came around the time Bayern Munich were interested in then-Chelsea winger Callum Hudson-Odoi, who shared the same agent as Musiala, who moved from Germany to England when he was seven.

Bayern were already aware of Musiala because he was born in Germany, but the timing was right to make a deal happen.

"There were for sure some pieces that came together at that time," Sauer says.

"I think one reason why we fought for the player at that time was the reason we had the feeling that Chelsea is not really seeing his full potential to be a top player for their first team.

"Because, otherwise, if they would have seen him as a future prospect, then it would been hard, even for Bayern Munich, to get a player out of the Chelsea environment."

Other young players in the first-team squad include 18-year-old Bara Sapoko Ndiaye, signed from Gambinos Stars Africa in The Gambia, and 18-year-old Lennart Karl, who joined the academy four years ago and has been capped by Germany.

Shirts with Bayern's academy graduates adorn the walls of their youth campus

The Bayern Campus can house up to 43 players in accommodation, predominantly local players before they widen the search overseas.

"I think there is basically kind of a guideline that we want to have a minimum 60% of the players coming from the region and reaching the level of the under-19 age group," Sauer says.

"This automatically means that the other 40% of the team has to be recruited from other regions nationwide.

"Coming to an age group of under-17, we are also reaching out to the main European football markets to recruit the most talented players internationally.

"Jamal Musiala is one perfect example. As soon as we're coming to an age of 16 and the regulations allow us to do international transfers, we want to recruit the best talents in Europe. That's for sure part of our recruitment philosophy."

Another piece that fell into place for Musiala was the Bayern under-17 team at that time was coached by Miroslav Klose, the former Bayern forward who is the record goalscorer for Germany.

Klose is credited with pushing Musiala to work on the defensive side of his game. He also knew what a player needed to get to the highest level, with the former striker becoming an assistant to Hansi Flick when Musiala joined the first team.

That idea of having former players in charge of the next generation continues.

Ex-Bayern centre back Dante, who also played for Nice for more than 10 years, is the current under-19 head coach.

"They can inject a little bit of the Bayern Munich DNA into the players," Sauer explains. "More from a personality side, not necessarily from a playing style.

"He also has some different ideas on the playing style but you know playing for Bayern Munich and being in the first team of Bayern Munich, at least they can tell our players what they have to be from a character, from a personality to make it up to the first team."

With so many players coming into the system and a difficult first-team set-up to break into, the Bayern style remains consistent throughout age groups.

Coaches are given guidelines to work towards but it does not stop them from having their own ideas as they aim for a style of "dominance and intensity".

"But football is always a process of evaluation," Sauer says.

"Opening the campus in 2017, we have put a very clear idea of football in place, but always kept the openness to add in ideas from coaches like [Jupp] Heynckes, [Julian] Nagelsmann, [Thomas] Tuchel, Hansi Flick, and, for sure, [current Bayern manager Vincent] Kompany. The football is always developing.

"So we have to be open enough always to amend little things. But I would say that the overall strategy is still what it was in the times of Heynckes, Pep Guardiola or Louis van Gaal."

There is an eye-catching display in one of the well-kept corridors of Bayern's campus. Shirts of high-profile academy graduates are framed on the walls, with a display showing tiers of Germany's football leagues and players who have played in them.

To qualify for the display, players need to have played a minimum of 30 full 90-minute games.

Bayern say that almost 44% of the young players who are in their youth set-up until the under-19 team become a professional player.

"The success is not only bringing players to Allianz Arena, but bringing players also to professional football. This is also essential if you want to convince a young talented player to be part of Bayern Munich," Sauer adds.

"For us, it's more the story: Listen, if you're coming to Bayern Munich we cannot guarantee that you will be a first-team player at Bayern Munich, because it's very tough to achieve. And you have a lot of world-class players around you. So if you are a top striker and you have Harry Kane there it will be difficult to replace him.

"But what we can at least guarantee you is we can teach you and develop you to a level that you have a very, very big chance to be a professional football player at least in a tier one, tier two or tier-three club."

Like most things in modern football, the development of players also has to make business sense for the six-time European champions, who last won the Champions League in 2019-20.

"Being in a competition with Paris St-Germain, all the English and the Spanish clubs to win the Champions League, it would be almost unrealistic to say we want to have 11 players on the pitch that play for our academy," says Sauer.

"But I think if we can reach the goal that we always have five or six players steadily in the first team, that would be a great success.

"On the other side, and this is more I would say economical answer, we do not have the money of the English clubs. We do not have the TV money. To be still competitive over the next decade, I think we all also have to make money with our players."

Examples over the past two years include selling forward Mathys Tel to Tottenham, left-back Adam Aznou to Everton, midfielder Paul Wanner to PSV and striker Jonah Kusi-Asare to Fulham.

"So I would say [our] final goal would be to develop every year a player from our academy to the first team and probably sell some others for a significant amount.

"[That] would be something that is a combination that would help us on the one side to have a good and competitive Bayern Munich team and on the other side to be still competitive on a level with Man City, Liverpool, Madrid and Barcelona.

"So I think that's those two goals that we have, bring players to Allianz Arena and make money."

Umwe mu bami gakondo bazwi cyane muri Nigeria, Emir wa Daura, yahagaritswe mu kazi no mu ngendo z'akazi, nyuma y'uko umugenzi w'umukerarugendo ukomoka muri Pologne amushinje kumukorera ihohotera rishingiye ku gitsina.

Uyu mukerarugendo yavuze ko Umar Farouk Umar, ufite imyaka 92, yamufashe ku mabere ubwo yari yagiye gusura ahantu nyaburanga hagamijwe ubukerarugendo, kandi ko ibyo yamukoreye byamuteye kumva abangamiwe cyane.

Ibi birego byateje impaka n'ibiganiro byinshi ku mbuga nkoranyambaga, aho abantu benshi basabaga ko Emir ahagarikwa ku mirimo ye ndetse hakaba iperereza kuri ibyo birego.

Leta ya Katsina yamaze kubahiriza icyo cyifuzo.

Umar ntaragira icyo atangaza ku birego aregwa cyangwa ku ihagarikwa rye.

Ni umwe mu ba Emir benshi, bafite umwanya gakondo uhabwa agaciro cyane kuva mbere y'ubukoloni, bakaba bagikomeje kugira uruhare rukomeye mu muco no mu idini mu majyaruguru ya Nigeria, n'ubwo batakigira ububasha bwa politiki bari bafite mu bihe byashize.

Umujyi wa Daura, aho Umar akorera inshingano ze nka Emir, ufite agaciro gakomeye cyane ku bwoko bw'aba Hausa, biganje mu majyaruguru ya Nigeria.

Uyu mujyi ufatwa nk'ahantu hera kandi hafite amateka akomeye ku ba Hausa, ndetse ukaba ari na ho inkomoko y'ubwami bwabo gakondo iherereye.

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Daura kandi ni umusingi w'amateka n'imyemerere y'ubwo bwoko ku bijyanye n'inkomoko yabo, ndetse n'ishingiro ry'ubuyobozi gakondo bwemewe muri uwo muco.

Abanyapolitiki bakunze gusura ibwami kwa Emir kugira ngo abasabire imigisha kandi banashake ubufasha n'inkunga ye.

Ku rubuga rwe rwa Instagram, uyu mukerarugendo yavuze ko yari amaze iminsi 30 azenguruka Nigeria mbere yo gusura ibwami kwa Emir ku itariki ya 14 Ugushyingo (11).

Yashyizeho amashusho yaje gusibwa nyuma yaho, agaragaza umugabo usa na Emir amufashe amaboko ayashyize ku bibero bye.

Hashize akanya gato, humvikanye uyu mugore avuga ati: "Rekera aho! rekera aho!", mu gihe uwo mugabo yari atangiye kumukora ku gituza.

Nk'uko byatangajwe mu itangazo, Guverineri wa Leta ya Katsina, Dikko Umaru Radda, yategetse ko hashyirwaho komite ako kanya, kugira ngo ikore iperereza kuri ibyo birego.

Iryo tangazo ryavuze ko ubuyobozi bwa Leta bufata ibyo birego nk'ikibazo gikomeye kandi ko buzashingira ku byavuye mu iperereza rya komite kugira ngo hafatwe icyemezo gikwiye.

Ryakomeje rivuga ko ibizava mu iperereza n'ibyifuzo bya komite bizashyirwa mu bikorwa uko byakabaye, rishimangira ko ubutabera buzubahirizwa.

Icyakora, iryo tangazo ntiryagaragaje amazina y'abagize komite ishinzwe iperereza, inshingano zayo mu buryo burambuye cyangwa igihe yagenewe gutanga raporo y'ibyo izaba yabonye.

Uyu Emir amaze imyaka myinshi ku ngoma, kuko yagiye ku ntebe y'ubwami mu mwaka wa 2007, asimbuye murumuna we witwaga Bashar dan Umaru, wari umaze imyaka 41 ayoboye.

MN202611_vrir45bnkz.t:
Panoramic view of Mbabane, the capital city of Eswatini in southern Africa

The UK forcibly resettled a refugee and convicted sex offender in an African country with which he had no connection, in a deal not disclosed to the UK Parliament or the local community.

The man, who was from Sri Lanka and had a history of severe mental illness and suicide attempts, took his own life months after arriving in Eswatini.

The BBC has obtained a copy of the draft deal between the two governments, in which the UK pledges to cover the costs of his resettlement for up to three years.

The UK government was finalising plans for 35-year-old Kishanth Peramalya to live there permanently when he died.

Migration experts told the BBC this was the first known case of the UK government forcibly resettling in such a manner a refugee permanently overseas.

In 2024, the Labour government scrapped a controversial plan to send asylum seekers with pending claims to Rwanda. Now it wants to send failed asylum seekers overseas to third countries when they cannot be sent to their home countries, but is yet to announce any deals. Last week, five EU countries reached a deal to send people whose claims have been refused to Rwanda.

The Eswatini deal raises questions about how much the UK government should disclose about such arrangements, and how it protects both the people it sends overseas and the communities that receive them.

The UK government told the BBC that protecting the British public was its priority and that it "continue[s] to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case".

Peramalya's family is demanding answers about his treatment, while critics in Eswatini have accused Britain of using their country as a "dumping ground".

In 2021, the Royal Navy rescued Peramalya in the Indian Ocean, along with dozens of other Sri Lankan asylum seekers, as they tried to sail from India to Canada.

They were then detained in a camp on Diego Garcia, an island in the British Indian Ocean Territory, run exclusively as a UK-US military base.

The island's authorities, who answer to London, recognised that Peramalya and others could not safely return to Sri Lanka, and awarded them refugee protections. But the group remained in the camp for three years while British officials debated their future. A court later ruled their detention had been unlawful.

Tamils were detained in a camp on Diego Garcia

As a teenager, Peramalya had been tortured and sexually abused by officers in the Sri Lankan military and was later diagnosed with PTSD. During his detention on Diego Garcia, his mental health deteriorated, according to court papers. He suffered from depression and anxiety, and repeatedly attempted suicide. UN inspectors who came to the island raised concerns over the conditions he was being kept in.

While there, he committed a series of crimes, including assault and arson, during two suicide attempts, and spent 24 weeks in prison. He was also convicted of four counts of sexual assault for which he received a suspended prison sentence.

In December 2024, most of the Sri Lankan asylum seekers were allowed to enter the UK but ministers refused to let Peramalya join them because of his crimes. He remained on Diego Garcia.

The High Court upheld the UK's refusal to admit him, in part because of the risk he posed and because ministers were making genuine efforts to find somewhere else safe for him to live. Court documents, seen by the BBC, show the UK approached more than 20 countries and could not secure an agreement.

Then, in February 2026, the US began using its military base on Diego Garcia in its war with Iran. The island authorities began withdrawing non-essential personnel.

At the end of March, the Maldives offered to take Peramalya for 30 days. He was transferred there before being sent on to Eswatini, formerly known as Swaziland.

At the time of his death, the British and Eswatini governments had been finalising the agreement for Peramalya to live there permanently, with the UK to pay for the "reasonable costs" of his accommodation, healthcare, and other support for up to three years.

The document does not specify a total cost or explain how the two governments would manage the risks Peramalya posed to himself and others. But it explicitly acknowledged he required support that would meet his basic needs and protect his physical and mental health, and wellbeing.

Peramalya's family has told the BBC he was initially placed in an isolated guesthouse on his own.

Speaking from India, his sister said the family had not been aware of the plan to make his transfer permanent, and that his mental health had worsened while in the country.

She said he would call her four times a day. "My brother did not want to go there at all," she said. "He couldn't manage being there alone, he was very lonely." The family also said it had been unaware of sexual offences committed by him.

He initially saw a psychiatrist weekly, she said. Later, after his mental health declined, he had daily appointments, and an attendant was brought in to prepare his food.

The UN's refugee agency, which had previously raised concerns about Peramalya's condition on Diego Garcia, said it was "deeply saddened" by his death and stressed that refugees being transferred to other different countries must be protected.

"UNHCR recognises that asylum seekers and refugees may, in certain circumstances, be lawfully transferred to a third country. However, this requires that specific safeguards are in place and those conditions are fulfilled in practice."

Peter Walsh, of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, described the case as "highly unusual".

"In most cases, people with criminal convictions who cannot be returned to their home country would simply remain in the UK. Third countries are generally quite reluctant to accept foreign national offenders," he said.

It is unclear how Britain chose Eswatini, but the kingdom had already agreed to accept US deportees under President Trump's wider programme of sending migrants to countries across Africa and Latin America. In 2025, the Trump administration paid Eswatini $5.1m (£3.9m) to accept up to 160 people.

Melusi Simelane, of the Southern African Litigation Centre, who is challenging the US deal in court, said migrant transfers were putting pressure on his country's limited resources.

"Our healthcare system is crumbling, not to mention our mental healthcare, so it is a big ask to bring people into our society who need a lot of support," he said.

"Africa is becoming a dumping ground for the world's unresolved problems."

Zakithi Sibandze, of the Eswatini Rural Women's Assembly, which campaigns to protect women and girls, said it was "very painful" that a sex offender had been relocated to her country.

"Why did they think it was okay to send him to Africa?" she asked. "The UK seems to be saying it is fine for people to commit crimes against women in poor countries."

Earlier this year, the UN's special rapporteur on migrants' rights, Gehad Madi, urged governments to publish the terms of their migration arrangements with other countries and subject them to parliamentary and public oversight. "Strengthening transparency is essential to reduce human rights risks, ensure accountability and uphold the rule of law," he said.

Neither the UK nor Eswatini authorities answered the BBC's questions on the circumstances surrounding Peramalya's resettlement, but a spokesperson for the British government said: "Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people. That includes taking steps to ensure high-harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK."

Additional reporting by Alice Cuddy and Swaminathan Natarajan

MN202611_1ocf4x881e2.t:
The museum's Our Time space will host events among 13 large installations and flocks of sheep benches

Ten years ago the Museum of London announced it would be leaving its former home to move to the abandoned halls of Smithfield Market. Now rebranded London Museum, it is set to open its doors to the public on Saturday after a £437m project. So what's it like inside?

Leaning back on a leather sofa, museum director Sharon Ament looks across a vast brick-lined space that once bustled with market traders but is now filling with its newest visitors.

"I really love this space, it just makes me smile every time I come in - it's actually joyful," she says.

The vast room, now known as Our Time, is dotted with installations reflecting living memory.

In one corner a life-size mechanical giraffe flicks its ears in front of a lit-up NHS sign representing lockdown. Another wall has remnants of London's former greyhound tracks. Near it is the old switchboard from Buckingham Palace.

And beneath the magnificent domed ceiling roam several flocks of large plastic sheep which Ament encourages people to "pull up and take a seat" on.

"There are grins on people's faces, so I think we've pulled something rather incredible off," she says.

Sharon Ament says she wants the museum to be a shared space for everyone

The museum reflects London's more recent history such as its greyhound-racing tracks - the fireplaces of the market traders' former offices can be seen behind

A visit to the new museum starts before this point as people enter through a large covered street known as Real Time.

Here, data-filled digital displays tell of London in the moment, beside a Banksy-graffitied sentry box and the last bell to be cast at the historic Whitechapel Bell Foundry .

Next they enter the former General Market with its sheep, giraffe and signage.

This is the space where events like late-night house parties and dinner clubs will be held beside shops and eateries, including former Victorian cocoa rooms that will be open 24 hours a day at weekends.

Such hints of the building's past are everywhere. Halfway up the walls are the restored fireplaces of the traders' former offices, along with twisting metal staircases that once led up to them.

"Whenever we've found historic fabric, we've restored it or kept it, and we want to show the layers of history," explains Alec Shaw, who has led the entire project.

"We wanted a museum that worked like the market, that allowed you to come in any corner and just walk across, walk through the building on your way to work, or, hopefully, stay a bit longer."

Smithfield's General Market opened in the 1880s and was in use until the 1990s

The Our Time space seen in early 2024 when water was still splashing into the building

Shaw previously showed me around the site nearly three years ago , when scaffolding and supports were holding up the walls and there were constant splashes of water dripping on to the floor.

Restoring a Victorian relic that was abandoned in the 1990s "really tested all of us", he admits, and that was before the logistics involved in designing a new museum from the venue's seven-million object collection.

Five thousand of these are now on site and another 300,000 are due to arrive for when the former Poultry Market becomes a museum space in 2028.

"We think you could take at least eight hours to see every object downstairs, and that means you're going to keep coming back.

"The best museums are those that you go, 'Right I'll do that one today. I'll do this gallery next time,'" he says.

Our Past is based in the building's basement and tells a weaving story of London through five different chapters

Queen Victoria's mourning dress is among the objects on display

A wide staircase to one side descends into what is called Past Time.

Down here is what once was street level of Roman London, and curator Annette Day explains that "we felt that right in the guts, in the earth of the city, that was the place where we should explore London".

A weaving route beneath a seven-metre-high brick vaulted ceiling tells the capital's story.

It starts with the city's creation by the Romans and moves through medieval times and London's place as the centre of the British Empire, before ending with the 2012 Olympic Games, a time when "London looked at itself and the world looked at London", says Day.

Along the way are all manner of objects.

There's Charles I's execution vest, Queen Victoria's mourning dress, a white 1960s Ford Cortina, an overstuffed taxidermy cat called Oliver and the shimmering Elizabethan jewellery of the Cheapside Hoard.

Large illustrations are incorporated with historic objects to tell the story of the Great Fire of London

Oliver the overstuffed taxidermy cat was once a Londoner's pet

Galleries on either side also focus on specific moments.

One features a recreated Roman room with amphoras - two-handled jars - a mosaic floor and the pieces of a magnificent wall painting found in Lime Street 20 years ago that hang on the wall.

Another uses large comic illustrations based on new research to tell the story of the Great Fire of London in an attempt to reflect the subject's inclusion in Key Stage 1 of the national curriculum.

Further along still, two other archways branch off to look at the lives of Londoners and the city's landscape, placing objects from across the ages alongside each other.

The delicately feathered Dying Swan outfit worn by lauded Russian dancer Anna Pavlova stands beside the stage outfit of Edwardian music hall star Kitty Lord in one case, while another shows 2,000 years of London-made shoes.

One case is even filled with toilets and chamber pots from medieval times to today.

And to carry on that subject, on the far wall a small porthole frames a chunk of the eponymous Whitechapel fatberg , not far from the huge glass window that looks out on passing Thameslink trains (whose passengers apparently are yet to notice they are now being watched).

Visitors can while away the hours watching Thameslink trains pass by the galleries

The museum has a small chunk of the Whitechapel fatberg, which weighed 130 tonnes and stretched more than 250m along a sewer

Even with its planned events, shops and eateries, Ament says it is all these objects which remain "the essence of the museum" because they "tell stories in a compelling way".

She sees the museum as a shared space for everyone, somewhere for Londoners and tourists alike to connect with people and stories from the past and now.

"Think of this as like one of my favourite buses, the number 63 bus. You meet the world on it. And you meet the world in here."

Most important of all, she says, is that the London Museum must always represent and reflect the city it is in.

"The story of London is tough and joyful at the same time. That's why we use 'grit and glitter' as a tagline - it's both of those things, those dualities can exist. And we shouldn't be frightened of that history," she says.

"We are making a museum and it will never stop, just like London never stops. There's always cranes in London and there'll always be new things in London Museum."

Visitors to Our Time are watched over by a life-sized giraffe model that flicks its ears

MN202611_15phl8tahpn.t:
Abasirikare b'Uburusiya 490.334 bamaze gupfa kuva intambara yo muri Ukraine yatangira mu mwaka wa 2022, nk'uko bigaragazwa n'imibare ya leta y'u Burusiya yasesenguwe na BBC.

Ni amakuru yashyizwe hanze, bivugwa ko byakozwe n'abinjiriye Rosstat, ikigo cy'u Burusiya gishinzwe ibarurishamibare, agaragaza uburyo igitero gikomeye cyagabwe kuri Ukraine cyahinduye imiterere y'impfu mu Burusiya.

Agaragaza kandi igiciro gikomeye cyishyuwe mu buzima bw'abantu ku ntambara Perezida Vladimir Putin yari yaratekereje ko izamara iminsi mike gusa, ariko ubu ikaba igiye kumara hafi imyaka itanu.

Ishami rya BBC ry'Abarusiya ryabonye inyandiko zirenga miliyoni 11 z'impfu zabaye hagati ya 2021 na Nzeri 2026, nyuma y'igitero cy'ikoranabuhanga cyagabwe n'itsinda ry'Ababelarusi rizwi nka Cyber Partisans BY hamwe n'itsinda ryo muri Ukraine ryitwa Silent Crow.

Rosstat yemeye ko yagabweho igitero cy'ikoranabuhanga, ariko ihakana ko hari amakuru y'ibanga yasohotse.

Ku bufatanye n'ikinyamakuru cyigenga cyo mu Burusiya Mediazona, BBC yasesenguye ayo makuru iyagereranya n'urutonde rw'abasirikare byemejwe ko bapfuye ku rugamba, nk'uko byakusanyijwe mu makuru afunguye kuva intambara yatangira.

Izo nyandiko zigaragaza ko 65% by'Abarusiya bafite imyaka hagati ya 18 na 24 bapfuye mu 2025 baguye ku rugamba rwo muri Ukraine.

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Mu bafite imyaka hagati ya 25 na 34, uwo mubare wari 59%.

Mu bafite imyaka hagati ya 45 na 54 gusa, ni ho indwara z'umutima n'imitsi zishe abantu benshi kurusha intambara.

Aya makuru anagaragaza ubukana bw'imfu z'abasirikare b'u Burusiya mu duce dutandukanye twa Ukraine.

Abasirikare bagera ku 20.000 bapfuye barwanira kwigarurira imidugudu 10 ya Ukraine yari ituwe n'abaturage 12.000 mbere y'intambara.

Mu rugamba rwo gufata umudugudu muto wa Andriivka, uri mu majyepfo y'umujyi wa Bakhmut mu karere ka Donetsk, abasirikare b'u Burusiya 1.122 bahasize ubuzima.

Mbere y'intambara, uwo mudugudu wari utuwe n'abantu 74 gusa.

Uburusiya ntibutangaza ku mugaragaro umubare w'abasirikare bwatakaje kuva intambara yatangira muri Gashyantare 2022.

Byongeye kandi, hashize imyaka ibiri Rosstat ihagaritse gutangaza imibare y'impfu zituruka ku mpamvu zo hanze y'uburwayi, yari isanzwe ikoreshwa mu kugereranya igipimo cy'abasirikare baguye ku rugamba.

Urugero, mu basirikare bakomoka mu turere twa Donetsk na Luhansk two mu burasirazuba bwa Ukraine twigaruriwe n'Uburusiya, kandi bakarwanira mu ngabo z'Uburusiya, BBC yasanze 70% gusa by'impfu zabo ari zo zagaragaye muri dosiye za Rosstat, bivuze ko hari izindi nyinshi zishobora kuba zitabaruwe muri ayo makuru.

Imibare y'ibanga y'Uburusiya yashyizwe hanze ishobora kuba ituzuye, ariko iyo ihujwe n'ubushakashatsi bwakozwe na BBC Russian, igaragaza amakuru afite akamaro gakomeye.

Abahanga mu bya gisirikare bavuga ko imibare ya BBC igaragaza abantu 290,012 bapfuye, yakusanyijwe hifashishijwe amakuru aboneka ku mugaragaro, ishobora kuba ihagarariye hagati ya 45% na 55% by'umubare nyakuri w'abasirikare b'Uburusiya bamaze gupfa.

Ibi bivuze ko umubare nyakuri ushobora kuba uri hagati ya 527,295 na 644,471.

Ugereranyije n'intambara y'Abasoviyeti muri Afghanistan yarangiye mu mwaka wa 1989, iyi mibare ni myinshi cyane ku Burusiya, cyane cyane ko iyi ntambara imaze imyaka ine n'amezi 10.

Icyakora, muri iyi mibare y'abapfuye muri iki gihe hashobora kuba harimo n'abanyamahanga barwanaga ku ruhande rw'Uburusiya.

Ku ruhande rwa Ukraine, Perezida Volodymyr Zelensky yari aherutse gutangaza muri Nyakanga(7) 2026 ko abasirikare ba Ukraine bamaze gupfa bagera ku 50,000.

Icyakora, urundi rutonde rwakozwe n'urubuga rwa UA Losses rutamenyekanye abarukoresha, rushingiye ku makuru aboneka ku mugaragaro, rwo rugaragaza ko umubare w'abasirikare ba Ukraine bapfuye ugera ku 115,952.

Rwanda is stepping up efforts to position avocado as a major foreign exchange earner, with industry stakeholders exploring strategies to increase production, improve quality, attract investment and expand access to international markets.

Avocado growers, exporters and officials from the National Agricultural Export Development Board (NAEB) have convened for a three-day meeting to examine opportunities and challenges across the avocado value chain.

The meeting, which also brings together members of the Horticulture Exporters Association of Rwanda (HEAR), seeks to develop strategies covering the entire production chain, from cultivation and harvesting to processing, packaging and international distribution.

NAEB Deputy Chief Executive Officer in charge of Operations, Sandrine Urujeni, said the institution is committed to working with government agencies, development partners and private sector players to accelerate the commercial development of avocado farming.

“Our objective is not merely to increase the number of avocado trees or expand the acreage under cultivation, but to develop a productive, commercially competitive, quality-driven and market-oriented value chain capable of consistently supplying competitive products to both domestic and international markets,” Urujeni said.

Participants will examine findings from an avocado farming census expected to provide a comprehensive picture of the industry’s performance, identify existing gaps and inform future investment decisions.

The findings are also expected to guide interventions aimed at increasing productivity, strengthening value addition and diversifying export destinations.

With growing global demand for avocados, particularly in Europe, the Middle East and Asia, Rwanda has an opportunity to expand its footprint in the international horticultural market.

However, competing with established avocado exporters such as Kenya, South Africa, Mexico and Peru will require more than increased production.

International buyers demand consistent volumes, strict phytosanitary compliance, traceability, proper harvesting techniques, reliable cold-chain infrastructure and adherence to international food safety standards.

Rwanda’s geographical position as a landlocked country also makes transport costs and logistics critical factors in determining the competitiveness of its exports.

Beyond exporting fresh fruit, the avocado industry presents opportunities for investment in processing facilities producing avocado oil, cosmetics and other high-value products. Such investments could reduce post-harvest losses, create employment, increase farmers’ incomes and retain more economic value within the country.

For Rwanda, developing a commercially viable avocado industry also fits into the broader national ambition of diversifying exports, reducing the trade deficit and strengthening foreign exchange reserves.

The ultimate challenge, therefore, is not simply how many avocados Rwanda can grow, but how much economic value the country can extract from every kilogram it produces.

Lincoln City have sacked their head coaches Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw just six months after they took joint charge of the Championship side.

The pair departed a little over 12 hours after they oversaw a 4-0 defeat at fellow strugglers Charlton Athletic on Tuesday.

The loss leaves the Imps just three points above the relegation places in what is the club's first season back in the second tier for 65 years.

Cohen and Shaw were assistant coaches under Michael Skubala when Lincoln were promoted as League One title winners last season.

They were surprisingly promoted to replace their boss as a joint managerial double act.

MN202611_1casrot0tmz.t:
Mu nama ya ‘YouthConnect Africa’ 2026, irimo kubera i Kigali kuri uyu wa Gatatu tariki 25 2026, uyoboye ibiganiro yasabye Perezida Kagame, kuvuga ku mpinduka yakwifuriza Abanyafurika cyangwa se uko yifuza ko Afurika yazaba imeze mu 2063.

Asubiza icyo kibazo, Perezida Kagame yagize ati, “ Dukeneye kubona impinduka mu mibanire dufitanye n’ibindi bice by’isi. Dukeneye kubona iterambere, dukeneye kubona uburumbuke,ndetse dukeneye kubona Abanyafurika atari bo bahora bategereje kwakira ibyo bagenerwa k’ubugiraneza bw’ibindi bice by’Isi.Kuko aho turahatinze cyane”.

“Tuhamaze igihe kinini ku buryo, binababaza cyane kubona uko Abanyafurika bagera ku bintu by’indashyikirwa, ariko kugira ngo bahabwa umwanya bakwiye kuba barimo, bigasaba ko bibanza kwemezwa n’undi muntu. Ibi rero tugomba kubihagarika. Ntitwakomeza dutyo. Kandi ni nk’aho abantu babifashe nk’ibisanzwe ku Banyafurika. Kandi ndizera ko urubyiruka, mu by’ukuri ruzahindira iyo myumvire imeze ityo,ko Afurika kuri buri kintu cyose, igomba kubanza kunyura muri gahunda yo kwemererwa n’umuntu runaka uri ahantu runaka,kandi ni nkaho byabaye ibintu bihoraho. Dukeneye guhagarika iyo mikorere nta gushidikanya”.

Perezida Kagame yashimangiye ko abazaba bahari mu 2063, nawe arimo, bakwiye kuzaba bafite ishema ry’uko hari impinduka zabayeho nziza muri Afurika kandi zikabaho zigizwemo uruhare n’Abanyafurika ubwabo, bashyizeho urubuga rwabo rwiza, aho guhora bagaburirwa, cyangwa se ngo bahore bagomba kubanza kwisobanura ku bandi bantu runaka, mbere yo kugira icyo ari cyo cyose bakora.

Yagize ati, “ Ku bazaba bahari mu 2063,kandi nanjye nshobora kuzaba mpari nubwo bimeze bityo(…),nibura tugomba kuzaba turi aho dufite ishema ryo kuvuga tuti impinduka zabayeho, kandi zabayeho zishingiye ku mbaraga zacu, no gukorera hamwe, tugakora uko dushoboye kugira ngo tugire iryo shema ryo kuba Abanyafurika barashyizeho ahantu habo, urubuga rwabo, badasabwa guhora batanga ibisobanuro muri byose”.

“Ubu turagaburirwa,duhora twibutswa ko tugomba kuba mu mwanya wacu,kandi bitugabanyiriza icyubahiro. Ngira ngo uru rubyiruko nturwishimiye ibyo bintu. Rero nimugire icyo mubikoraho. Urubyiruko rukeneye gukorera hamwe, rukeneye kumenya ko muri rwo harimo ibyo rukeneye kandi ni bimwe n’ibyo abandi bantu bifitemo byatumye banazamuka bakagera ku rwego ruturi hejuru, nubwo atari ko byagombye kumera”.

MN202611_1qmw5ouo33g.t:
Ffion Morgan joined West Ham from Bristol City in 2025

Wales and West Ham winger Ffion Morgan is facing a lengthy spell on the sidelines after suffering an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury.

Morgan has undergone surgery having been helped off during West Ham's Women's Super League win over Charlton earlier this month.

The 26-year-old is now likely to miss the rest of the season.

"Ffion will now begin her rehabilitation programme under the supervision of the club's medical team," a West Ham statement said.

The injury also makes Morgan a major doubt for next summer's Women's World Cup, should Wales qualify.

Rhian Wilkinson's side take on Norway in a two-legged play-off final next week as they bid to reach the tournament for the first time in the nation's history.

Morgan, who has 56 caps, is an international regular and would be a shoo-in for the Wales squad if fit.

Five return for Wales' World Cup play-off final

Home World Cup can inspire Wales' future stars

She joined West Ham on a two-year deal in 2025 after her contract at Bristol City expired.

Morgan has also played for Cardiff City, Coventry United and Crystal Palace.

She suffered an ACL injury while playing for Wales Under-19s as a teenager, while she had only recently returned to action for West Ham after another lengthy fitness lay-off.

Wales face Norway at the Cardiff City Stadium on Tuesday, 1 December, before the return leg in Oslo four days later.

Wales are hoping to cause an upset as they bid to reach the Women's World Cup for the first time, though beating former champions Norway may not be enough to guarantee a place in Brazil next summer.

The complex nature of the qualification process means that Wales may have to negotiate inter-confederation play-offs next February to secure a World Cup place, even if they triumph over Norway.

China has sent a Pakistani astronaut along with two Chinese astronauts onto its Shenzhou-24 mission, marking the first time a foreign national has set foot aboard the Tiangong space station.

The landmark moment for 40-year-old air force pilot Muhammad Zeeshan Ali highlights China's desire for its space station to become an international research facility.

The mission is expected to last for several days before returning to Earth.

MN202611_jj37s3lfsx.t:
Umuyobozi w’Urugaga rw’Abakiri Bato Bakora Ubucuruzi muri Cameroon, Isidore Kameu, yavuze ko yifuza kubona umuziki w’u Rwanda ugera mu bindi bihugu bya Afurika, asaba abahanzi b’Abanyarwanda kurushaho gukorana n’abo ku mugabane.

Kameu, usanzwe ari umuproducer (utunganya imiziki) akaba n’umuyobozi w’abahanzi, wari usuye u Rwanda ku nshuro yambere, yabivugiye mu nama ya YouthConnekt Africa Summit, yavuze ko ibyo yabonye mu gihugu byamushimishije kandi bikamwereka isura nshya y’Afurika.

Yavuze ko u Rwanda rwamubera urugero rw’ubudacogora, ashimangira ko isuku, ubwiza n’imyitwarire y’Abanyarwanda yabonye bishobora kumenyekana kurushaho binyuze mu muziki n’ubundi buhanzi.

Yagize ati “Birababaje ko ari ukuza mu Rwanda byatumye menya ko ari igihugu cyiza, gifite isuku kandi Abanyarwanda bafite imyitwarire myiza.”

Kameu yavuze ko umuziki n’umuco bishobora gufasha Afurika guhindura uko isi iyibona, asaba urubyiruko cyane cyane abakora mu muziki gukoresha impano zabo mu kugeza iyi shusho nshya ku bandi.

Ati “Binyuze mu buhanzi, umuco n’umuziki, dushobora kugira isura nshya y’uko turi kandi tukayereka isi.”

Uyu muproducer yavuze ko yifuza ko umuziki w’u Rwanda wamenyekana muri Cameroon no mu bindi bihugu byo muri Afurika, ndetse ko abahanzi b’Abanyarwanda bakwiye kugira imikoranire myinshi n’abahanzi bo mu tundi turere tw’umugabane.

Ati “Nifuza ko abahanzi b’u Rwanda bakorana, atari ku rwego rw’akarere gusa, ahubwo no muri Afurika yose. Nifuza ko umuco w’u Rwanda wumvikana muri Cameroon.”

Yavuze ko kandi yifuza kubona abahanzi b’Abanyarwanda bakomeye muri muzika na sinema bakorana n’abahanzi bo muri Afurika yo Hagati, kugira ngo impano z’Afurika zirusheho kugenda hagati y’ibihugu.

Kameu kandi yashimye kuba u Rwanda rwarafunguye imipaka yarwo ku Banyafurika, avuga ko ibi bishobora gutanga amahirwe yo kurushaho guhuza urubyiruko, abahanzi n’abandi bakora mu nganda ndangamuco.

Mu gusubiza Kameu, Perezida Paul Kagame yavuze ko igitekerezo cyo guhuza abahanzi n’inzego zishinzwe umuco mu bihugu bitandukanye bya Afurika gishobora gushyirwa mu bikorwa, hakoreshejwe inzego zisanzwe zihari.

Yavuze ko ibihugu bifite inzego zishinzwe umuco n’ubuhanzi, bityo ko izo nzego zikwiye gukorana no gufasha abantu bafite ibitekerezo nk’ibya Kameu kubishyira mu bikorwa.

Perezida Kagame yavuze ko atari ikibazo gikomeye nk’uko bamwe bashobora kubitekereza, ahubwo ko hakenewe ubushake bwo gufata iki kibazo nk’ingenzi.

Ati “Tugomba gusa kugifata nk’ikintu cy’ingenzi. Ntabwo binagoye nk’uko gukuraho inzitizi z’ubucuruzi bwambukiranya imipaka bigoye.”

Yavuze ko inzego bireba zishobora no gukomeza kuganira n’abahanzi n’abandi bakora mu bijyanye n’umuco kugira ngo harebwe uburyo ibyo bitekerezo byahinduka ibikorwa bifatika.

MN202611_14p6jmxzg3r.t:
John Motson was a legendary football commentator who covered 10 World Cups, 10 European Championships and 29 FA Cup finals for BBC Sport

Football game EA Sports FC will feature the digitally recreated voice of the late commentator John Motson, Electronic Arts has exclusively told the BBC.

Motson, who died in 2023, was the main commentator for BBC Sport for decades - and performed the same role for the video game series during the 90s and 00s.

It is the first time the hit series, formerly known as Fifa, has featured a deceased commentator.

With the permission of his widow and his son, Motson's voice has been synthesised using a combination of old recording sessions and generative AI. It will become available in FC 27 on 26 November.

The legendary commentator died aged 77 in February 2023 - several months before the launch of ChatGPT and the massive growth of AI it set in train.

Fred Motson told the BBC it "means an awful lot" to have his dad's voice in EA Sports FC once again.

"I grew up with Fifa," he said. "I always used to tell my parents that I needed the latest console for Christmas because otherwise dad couldn't see how the game worked."

Electronic Arts, which was bought for $55bn (£42bn) in August , would not say if it paid Motson's family, telling the BBC it does not "disclose the financial terms of our agreements".

WATCH: The new John Motson commentary in EA Sports FC 27 - and how it sounded back in Fifa 1998

John Motson was the first commentator for the series, appearing on games from Fifa 96 up to Fifa 2005. He later made a brief cameo in Fifa 19.

"While he completely understood when they went in a different direction, I think he really missed it after he left the game and it felt like a bit of an end of an era," his son said.

EA told the BBC the studio would not have included Motson in the game unless they had permission from his family.

"There was no way we would have moved forward with this in any way, shape or form if they weren't fully on board," said Mat Prior, senior game design director at EA Sports FC.

"At the outset we wanted to pay tribute to to Motty as the commentator and as this emotional connection - he was the very first voice of our game - so we really wanted to do him justice and bring him back."

He explained that Motson's voice in the game was a combination of old lines he recorded over the years and AI - tech which he said was "the only way" to make it happen, as they don't have recordings of him talking about modern players like Bradley Barcola and Chloe Kelly.

Gazza's tears, Radford's screamer & the Crazy Gang - 5 of Motty's best

Motson's son Fred said he believed his dad would have "absolutely" wanted to be involved in the game after his death.

"My dad was the least technological person in the world," he said. "Till his dying day, he had a typewriter on his desk.

"So I don't think he would have quite understood what the AI was doing technologically - but I think, on the other hand, he was always really keen to get involved in these kinds of projects."

But Peter Caulfield, founder of Save Our Voices Now which campaigns against AI voice cloning, expressed some disquiet about the project, and the fact Motson had been unable to consent to it.

"If someone has signed a deal allowing their likeness to be used after they die, I have no issue with that," he said.

"But in life or in death, unless you have specifically agreed to it, AI cloning of any kind should not be allowed.

"Being a family member shouldn't automatically give you that right either."

One of the main arguments against the use of generative AI in video games is that it can replace humans - something that EA was keen to argue against.

"From a gaming standpoint, it's something we've used for many years - like machine learning to help drive animation systems and so on and so forth," Prior said.

"It's not there to replace commentators in any way shape or form... there's certainly no future plans to replace anyone with AI."

Derek Rae, who has been a commentator in EA FC for several years, said the tech could make things easier, but he still spent a long time recording dialogue in studios.

"It's quite a lot of days in the course of a year," he said. "So it might be two or three times a month that we do it in season for the game, which is typically sort of November time through until May.

"The more creative things have to be done with the human voice because they have to have the personality, sometimes a little chuckle thrown in the middle of a sentence or a little idiosyncrasy," he said.

"But when it comes to the more normal features in a video game, for example, routine surnames like Smith and Jones and Brown, that's something that AI can probably accomplish quite easily."

Josko Gvardiol tackling Jamal Musiala in FC 27 - perhaps examples of some less routine surnames

Rae said he was excited about the Motson project - but wasn't convinced he would follow suit.

"If we're being modest, we might say, well, no, I don't want to inflict my voice on the next generation."

He told BBC News it was something he would need to "think about" it but added: "I'm hopefully many years away from having to make a decision like that."

MN202611_9z1ju3xj7t.t:
'We should win. You know that, I know that'

A squandered victory at the seaside has redefined Russell Martin's definition of frustration.

The Leicester City manager said he was "hurt" by the solitary point his side picked up in Tuesday's 1-1 draw at lowly Blackpool in League One after dominating just about every facet of the game – controlling 77% possession and amassing 30 shots, of which nine were on target.

Asked if the draw was the most frustrating moment of the season, former Rangers and Southampton boss Martin replied by saying: "This season? Of my short but feels like very long managerial career."

That says a lot coming from a manager who was smuggled out of the stadium under police escort then sacked at Rangers after a draw with Falkirk last season, and whose Southampton side was once undone in the Premier League by two second-half Mohamed Salah goals after leading 2-1.

Those were tenure-defining defeats for a manager whose reputation has taken a battering in recent seasons, with his style of possession-heavy, passing football – an approach he once said was to "dominate the ball and be aggressive with it" , external – coming in for particular ridicule when results have gone against his side.

It has been the same at one-time Premier League title winners Leicester this season in the third tier, with Martin's method called into question in the early months of his tenure after the Foxes got off to a slow start.

Results have improved in recent weeks - they are unbeaten in six matches across all competitions and are up to seventh in the table.

But victory would have had them within a point of the play-off places, and Martin said the result will leave him "eternally frustrated".

"We should win, I know that, you know that and I think everyone in the stadium knows that. But we don't," he told BBC Radio Leicester after the match at Bloomfield Road.

"How we only score one goal, I'm really struggling to come to terms with.

"We have brilliant chances in the middle of their goal, not like half chances. And we actually score a goal that is really brilliant, but we shouldn't need a goal like that to win the game.

"I'm not frustrated, I'm hurt that we don't win the game and we concede a rubbish goal."

Is Leicester boss Martin turning the Foxes' fortunes?

Listen to BBC Radio Leicester's When You're Smiling podcast

It took more than an hour for the Foxes to break Blackpool's resistance, with a deluge of chances missed before Will Alves cut in from the left to beat home goalkeeper Bailey Peacock-Farrell with a shot that took a slight deflection.

It was six minutes from the end when Niall Ennis scrambled home the leveller for the Seasiders.

"I'm really proud of the players and how much they have grown in terms of what the performances look like," said Martin.

"But it's my job to be demanding of them, and there is no way we should be drawing that game. No way."
