President Paul Kagame has urged young African entrepreneurs to embrace collaboration and strengthen partnerships to overcome challenges facing businesses, particularly in expanding their enterprises and accessing wider markets.

Speaking at the YouthConnekt Africa Summit 2026, Kagame noted that although nearly a quarter of Africa’s working-age population is engaged in business and entrepreneurship, significant challenges remain in growing businesses and turning entrepreneurial initiatives into successful enterprises.

He emphasised that building successful companies requires collective effort, shared ambition and cooperation rather than individual efforts.

“Remember that the big companies in the world were not built in isolation. They were built through collaboration, by people who shared a vision. We need to do the same,” Kagame said.

He encouraged young entrepreneurs to remain committed to their ambitions, work hard and invest their energy in building businesses capable of competing beyond their local markets.

“Work hard, put in the effort, and the world will be waiting for you. Our responsibility as leaders is to support you,” he added.

Kagame’s remarks highlighted the importance of creating an enabling environment in which young entrepreneurs can access opportunities, establish meaningful partnerships and scale their businesses.

His message comes as African countries seek to harness the continent’s youthful population as a driver of economic transformation, innovation and job creation.

MN202611_1mhwwbtawjr.t:
The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) has called for stronger support systems that connect young Africans’ ideas and ambitions to financing, markets and leadership opportunities, stressing that programmes alone are not enough to unlock the continent’s youth potential.

Dr. Matthias Naab, UNDP Director of the Regional Service Centre for Africa, made the call while addressing the YouthConnekt Africa Summit 2026 (YCA2026), where leaders, development partners and young innovators are meeting to discuss ways of advancing youth empowerment and economic opportunities across the continent.

Naab emphasised the need to move beyond isolated youth initiatives towards comprehensive ecosystems that enable young people to turn their ideas into viable enterprises, access markets and contribute meaningfully to development.

“Africa’s young people do not simply need programs, they need ecosystems that connect their ideas and ambitions to finance, markets, leadership opportunities and lasting impact,” he said.

His remarks highlight the importance of coordinated efforts by governments, development institutions and the private sector to create an enabling environment in which young Africans can access the resources, networks and opportunities needed to realise their potential.

With Africa home to one of the world’s youngest populations, strengthening youth entrepreneurship, access to finance and participation in decision-making remains central to unlocking the continent’s demographic dividend.

MN202611_4qigtjae11.t:
President Paul Kagame has urged African countries to strengthen collaboration, invest in local talent and develop the infrastructure needed to become equal partners in the global development of artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging technologies.

Speaking during the YouthConnekt Africa Summit 2026, Kagame said Africa has the human talent and technical expertise to participate meaningfully in developing advanced technologies rather than remaining a passive consumer of innovations produced elsewhere.

He noted that Africans are already working within some of the world’s leading technology companies, demonstrating that the continent has engineers, data analysts and innovators capable of contributing to the next generation of technological advancements.

“There is no reason why Africa should be disconnected from this when we actually have all these things. The only thing we need to do is to come together, deploy them, develop them, and make sure they work for us,” Kagame said.

The President emphasized the need for stronger partnerships between governments, the private sector and technology professionals, alongside greater investment in infrastructure, skills development and access to financing.

He also challenged African countries to reconsider their position in international technology partnerships, arguing that the continent should move beyond being a junior partner and take an equal role in shaping the technologies that increasingly influence economies and societies.

“We can’t always be the junior partners in everything. I think we have to be equal partners at one point,” he said.

Kagame called on young people, governments and businesses to take responsibility for mobilising the continent’s existing expertise and turning it into practical solutions that address Africa’s development challenges.

On artificial intelligence, he acknowledged its rapidly expanding potential to transform sectors such as medicine, agriculture and transportation, while warning that its benefits must be balanced against the risks associated with its use.

He stressed the importance of putting appropriate safeguards in place, particularly regarding safety, privacy and the responsible management of emerging technologies.

“AI is the way to go, but we need to put in place certain protections that will minimize the dangers they carry with them,” Kagame said.

He maintained that Africa has the capacity to benefit from technological advancement and shape its future, provided countries move beyond discussions and commit to meaningful cooperation, investment and implementation.

La Francophonie Secretary-General Louise Mushikiwabo (R) speaks to King Norodom Sihamoni of Cambodia at the opening ceremony of the gathering in his country

The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC)’s representatives are frantically filling social news studio that will have them, claiming “victory” at the recently concluded summit of the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF). The efforts are no more than a distraction from the actual result of what may come to be seen as a seminal moment in the organisation’s history.

The summit in the Cambodian capital of Phnom Penh, would most likely have returned the incumbent, Rwanda’s candidate, Louise Mushikiwabo, as OIF Secretary-General for a third term, but for tantrums by the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), threatening to quit the organisation, if she was re-elected.

So convinced it seems was the DRC that Mushikiwabo would emerge victorious, that to prevent her re-election they spared no effort in derailing the organisation’s processes for electing its head.

From the head of state, Felix Tshisekedi, to Minister of Communications, Patrick Muyaya, and foreign minister, Therese Kayikwamba Wagner, the DRC made clear it would go to any lengths to get what it wanted.

Rather than have one of their number turn an itnernational summit into an an unseemly spectacle, the other OIF members agreed a compromise that may have compromised the organisation’s rules, and the elections for the Secretary-General, were postponed for a year, at which time, the candidate that would almost certainly have won, would not present her candidature.

The DRC was right about one thing. Louise Mushikiwabo was running on an impressive record, and had the rules been followed, where if there is no consensus candidate, the Secretary-General is elected by a simple majority, it would have been difficult for any other candidate to have matched let alone surpass her.

Few would argue that in her two terms, Mushikiwabo made the OIF more effecient. Her administrative reforms streamedlined the organisation’s activities making it more effective. By the time she leaves office, the organisation’s resources will go farther, achieving more, in particular for women’s empowerment and support for young people.

No doubt taking from her many years as a minister in the RPF (Rwanda Patriotic Front) led government of Rwanda, she has reshaped the OIF to be more results orientated. The reforms have meant better qualified, more specialist positions for staff, clearer financial and administrative procedures, in general, a better run organisation.

Mushikiwabo has however, faced criticism that the organisation has not achieved as much on the international stage. But the criticism does not stand close scrutiny. Much of it clearly comes from the DRC, which without evidence, questions Mushikiwabo’s neutrality on matters to do with her native Rwanda.

Such a claim can be attributed to the DRC’s voluble campaign, to lay the blame for the crisis in the country, at Rwanda’s door, and in Congolese politicians’ eyes, neutrality would have meant full throated condemnation of Rwanda, from the OIF.

Critics also point out that it was on Mushikiwabo’s watch that OIF members Togo and Gabon, joined the Commonwealth, as well as Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger quitting the organisation. These criticisms too do not hold water. Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, left the organisation following coup d’etatas in their respective countries, and the rulers’ ire was directed more at France’s alleged colonial overreach than the OIF. It is a moot point whether Mushikiwabo or any other Secretary-General could have done more or anything at all, to keep them in the organisation.

As for Togo and Gabon, their membership of the Commonwealth need not affect their membership of the OIF. An arguably more rational criticism is that during her tenure, the OIF was largely invisible on the international stage.

While this may seem a perfectly reasonable criticism however, it overlooks the fact that the organisation has always had limited influence internationally, and her defence might be that it would have been difficult to have changed a position that has existed for all of fifty years, in two terms. And she may indeed argue that her reforms have strengthned the organisation’s foundations, upon which her successors can build to raise the oranisation’s influence internationally.

In fact, when the history of the OIF or perhaps that of the last summit is written, it will surely be noted that the very nature of the organisation will have been put on a more sustatainable footing, largely due to Rwanda’s contribution.

The delicate question of France’s position as de facto primus inter pares, needed to be addressed, and would in all likelihood have continued to be avoided, but for Rwanda lancing that boil.

When in an interview, Rwanda’s minister for foreign affairs and international cooperation, Oliviere Nduhungirehe commented on how he saw OIF, his remarks should be seen more as a statement of policy, or suggestion of policy, than just a response to a journalist’s question.

The “Francophonie is not about France” he said, “it’s an organisation of more that 90 countries, including 53 with full and equal rights, which share the same language. We should be united in promoting French language, as well as culture and economic cooperation. Most of all, we should not bring back the Francophonie of the old days, where a single country -France – was dictating its views to the rest of the community”

The comments followed a letter that France’s Emmanuel Macron reportedly sent to his Rwandan counterpart, Paul Kagame.

The letter, which has not been publicly released, is said to have directed rather than suggested, that in order to appease the DRC, Rwanda should withdraw its candidate for OIF Secretary-General, and endorse a consensus candidate, whom the DRC announced as Romania’s Dacian Ciolos.

We do know that the letter was sent from the Elise Palace to Urugwiro Village, and we can judge its peremptory tone by the reaction from Kigali. From what we know of Rwanda’s leadership, we can accurately deduce that we might never have heard of the letter, if it had been more appropriately worded, from one head of state to another. Kigali would have appreciated the need to discuss a thorny issue, and would have quietly, confidentially shared its own suggestions.

As it is, it seems that Kigali found it necessary to remind France that Rwanda, was a sovereign nation which should not be dictated to, and France only one country among many, which should not take it upon itself to give unilateral instructions to the other members.

Indeed, it has since emerged that the compromise to postpone the elections, was suggested by Rwanda.

The elephant being circled around in the room in Phnom Phenh, was of course, that like the Commonwealth, OIF, came into being as a colonial organisation, and it has had to adopt to the independence of former colonies.

While some in France might balk at Rwanda reminding them that the sovereignty of all member states must be given due regard, France may in the long run come to appreciate that the insistence strengthens the organisation, as a community of equal nations.

When, as part of her reforms, Mushikiwabo gives promotion of the French language and African languages, equal emphasis, she is in fact ensuring the sustainability of French in Africa. As Nduhungirehe, states, “the lesson we can take from this is that the Francophonie is a multilateral organisation with countries from almost all continents. It does not belong to France, and France cannot impose its views on our organisation.”

And when he further added that “the second lesson was that the organisation’s rules must be respected” that “the electoral rules adopted in Djerba, Tunisia had not been respected, despite having been approved by heads of state,” he was protecting the integrity of the organisation as a whole.

It is a virtual certainty therefore that at the next OIF summit, thanks in large measure to Rwanda’s interventions as to her own leadership, Mushikiwabo will hand over an organisation that will be more strengthened, effective, and more at peace with itself.

Vincent Gasana is a Senior Editorial Lead at Kigali Today Ltd. He spent many years at the BBC. He regularly write for KT Press

Huawei yagiriwe n'icaha co kwifatanya n'abandi mu kwiba amabanga y'ubudandaji no gukoresha uruyeri mu kwiba amabanki, ariko yezwa ku caha gikomeye kuruta ibindi co kugira uruhara mu bikorwa vy'ubugizi bwa nabi biteguwe mu ntumbero yo kuronka amafaranga bidaciye mu mategeko, mu rubanza rw'imbonekarimwe rwabereye muri Reta Zunze Ubumwe za Amerika.

Muri urwo rubanza rwamaze amezi abiri, abashikirizamanza bagirije ico kigo c'Abashinwa gikorera mu gisata c'ubuhinga bwa none no guhanahana amakuru ko cakoresheje ibinyoma, amanyanga n'ubusuma kugira kironke akarusho ku bandi bahiganwa na co.

Umurwi w'abunganira Huawei imbere y'amategeko wavuze ko abashikirizamanza bari bamaze gufata ingingo ko Huawei ari ikigo c'abagizi ba nabi, maze ibirego vyabo bavyubaka bahereye aho nyene. Ariko wo wemeza ahubwo ko iterambere ry'ico kigo ryavuye ku vyiyumviro bishasha cagiye kirazana mu bikorwa vyaco.

Huawei yavuze ko kuba yejejwe ku caha co kugira uruhara mu bikorwa vy'ubugizi bwa nabi biteguwe "vyemeza ko ivyo birego ata shingiro bifise mu vy'ukuri", yongerako ko izofata "ingingo zose zikenewe zemewe n'amategeko" kugira irwanire "uburenganzira n'inyungu" vyayo.

Abacamanza bari bashashe muri sentere yo mu gisagara ca Brooklyn, basanze Huawei yagirwa n'ivyaha 10 kuri 12 yakurikiranwako, harimwo icaha co kwifatanya n'abandi mu kurenga ku bihano reta ya Amerika yashizeho.

Ariko abo bacamanza baranse kwegeka kuri Huawei icaha co kwifatanya n'abandi mu bikorwa vy'ubugizi bwa nabi biteguwe mu ntumbero yo kuronka amahera mu buryo budahuye n'amategeko, icaha vyasaba ko babanza kwemeza ko ico kigo cakora nk'umurwi w'abagizi ba nabi.

Abashikirizamanza batangaje ubwa mbere ibirego vyerekeye Huawei mu 2019, inyuma y'uko umutegetsi nshingwabikorwa w'ico kigo, Meng Wanzhou, afatiwe muri Canada mu mpera za 2018, mu buryo bwakurikiwe kandi bwavuzweko cane.

Meng, azwi kandi nka Cathy Meng, yamaze imyaka itatu apfungiwe muri Canada, imbere y'uko arekurwa kugira asubire mu Bushinwa, biciye ku masezerano n'abashikirizamanza ba Amerika.

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Mu majambo yo gusozera urubanza mu ndwi iheze, icegera c'umushikirizamanza wa Amerika, Meredith Arfa, yabwiye abacamanza bari bashashe muri sentare ko Huawei yamaze imyaka 20 ikora ibishoboka vyose kugira yagure ubudandaji bwayo, muri ivyo hakaba harimwo kubesha amabanki ku bijanye n'ubudandaji bwayo muri Irani, hamwe no kwiba amabanga y'ubuhinga mu bindi bigo bihiganwa na yo, kugira ngo ironke akarusho mu guhiganwa.

Mw'itangazo, umushikirizamanza mukuru wa Amerika, Todd Blanche, yagize ati: "Mu myaka mirongo, Huawei n'ibigo bitatu biyishamikiyeko vyakorera imirimo ya vyo muri Leta Zunze Ubumwe za Amerika, vyishimikije ibinyoma n'ubusuma."

Yongeyeko ati: "Kubera ibikorwa vy'ibiro FBI bijejwe iperereza n'abashikirizamanza ba reta, ababigizemwo uruhara bazobibazwa."

Ariko umushingwamanza yunganira Huawei, Brian Heberlig, yavuze ko ico kigo cagutse mu budandaji bwaco kubera ibikorwa vy'umwete n'ubwitange. Ico kigo ubu gifise ibikorwa mu bihugu 170, kandi gikoresha abakozi barenga 200.000.

Inyuma y'uko urubanza ruciwe, Heberlig yabwiye BBC ko Huawei yanezerejwe n'uko abacamanza banse kuyegekako icaha co kugira uruhara mu bikorwa vy'ubugizi bwa nabi biteguwe.

Ati: "Ikirego gishingiye kuri RICO [itegeko ryo muri Amerika rirwanya ibikorwa vy'ubugizi bwa nabi biteguwe] cavuga ko Huawei ari ikigo kirangwa n'ibiturire, gifise umuco n'amategeko vy'imbere mu kigo bishingiye ku gukora ivyaha. Nk'uko tubibona, ico cari ikirego kirengeje urugero, kandi abacamanza bari bashashe baracanse mu buryo budasubirwamwo."

Yongeyeko ati: "Ni vyo, turafise ukwo twiyumva gutandukanye ku zindi ngingo zafashwe muri urwo rubanza… Twibaza ko Huawei yari ikwiye kwezwa ku vyaha vyose yakurikiranwako."

Vyitezwe ko urubanza ruzosomwa muri Nyakanga (9) 2027. Heberlig yavuze ko hazokorwa "ibikorwa bikomeye vyo gusaba" ko ico kigo gihabwa igihano gito gishoboka.

Yavuze kandi ko yiteze ko Huawei izokwunguruza urubanza.

Ati: "Ukwo nzi Huawei, urwo rugamba ruzobandanya, kandi iyo kompanyi ntizoruhuka gushika aho izoba yatanze ivyemezo vyose bishoboka ku rwego rw'iyungururizo, ikizera ko amaherezo izokwezwa."

MN202611_2z8ulcfata.t:
Tanzania’s Minister for Information, Culture, Arts and Sports, Paul Makonda, has projected that the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) could generate up to $2 billion in economic opportunities, urging businesses to prepare to benefit from the tournament.

Makonda made the remarks on November 25, 2026, during the launch of the Confederation of African Football (CAF) AFCON 2027 Finals Secretariat headquarters in Dar es Salaam, where he highlighted the tournament’s potential to transform tourism, trade, hospitality and other sectors.

The competition, branded PAMOJA AFCON 2027, will be jointly hosted by Tanzania, Kenya and Uganda, marking the first time three countries will jointly stage the continental football championship.

According to Makonda, the tournament is expected to feature 24 national teams playing 52 matches over 29 days, with approximately 1.8 million to two million spectators expected at eight stadiums across the three host countries.

Tanzania will host matches in Dar es Salaam, Arusha and Zanzibar, accounting for between 40 and 50 per cent of the tournament’s fixtures. The country expects to receive between 750,000 and 900,000 visitors, generating an estimated $2 billion in economic activity, equivalent to approximately five trillion Tanzanian shillings.

He said the anticipated benefits would extend beyond football, creating opportunities in accommodation, tourism, transportation, advertising and small and medium-sized businesses.

“The challenge will not be the market (demand), but our ability to supply that market. Therefore, we must strengthen ourselves, expand our businesses and services, and ensure they are ready,”Makonda said.

He urged entrepreneurs to formalise their businesses, establish an online presence and adopt internationally recognised digital payment systems to make their products and services accessible to international visitors.

He also encouraged businesses to invest in foreign-language skills, particularly English, French, Portuguese and Arabic, to improve their ability to serve visitors from across Africa and beyond.

Makonda emphasised that the success of the tournament should not be measured only by the quality of stadiums, goals scored or celebrations by supporters, but also by the jobs created, businesses expanded and improvements in people’s livelihoods.

“Our success will also be measured by the number of jobs we create, the businesses we grow, the tourists we attract and the lives of our citizens that we transform,” he said.

He further called on the three host countries to ensure that the economic benefits of the competition continue long after the final whistle.

“Let us not build stadiums and forget to build the economy. Let us not welcome visitors and forget to create opportunities. AFCON 2027 should end on the football pitches, but its impact should not end in our economies,” Makonda said.

The minister also praised Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu Hassan for her commitment to the preparations, saying she had directed government ministries to create favourable policy and legal conditions to ensure citizens benefit from hosting the tournament.

He described the launch of the secretariat offices as more than an administrative milestone, saying it marked a new chapter in sports development, East African cooperation and economic opportunities.

The tournament will also introduce Kiswahili as an official language of AFCON for the first time, according to Makonda, providing an opportunity to promote the language to international football audiences.

The 2027 edition will be particularly significant for East Africa, which is returning to host the continental championship after five decades, with Ethiopia having last hosted the competition in 1976.

Makonda concluded by welcoming CAF officials and football stakeholders to Tanzania, expressing confidence that the three host nations would deliver a memorable tournament while ensuring that its economic benefits reach ordinary citizens.

MN202611_knvg3r1wbp.t:
Rwanda is strengthening the use of data and evidence-based planning to improve healthcare delivery, with particular emphasis on integrating non-communicable diseases and other chronic conditions into community-based primary healthcare services.

The Minister of State in the Ministry of Health, Dr Yvan Butera, highlighted the country’s approach during a panel discussion on using data to inform evidence-based decision-making at the 2026 International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA), held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

Butera emphasised that reliable health data is essential in identifying population health needs, guiding resource allocation and ensuring that healthcare interventions respond to the realities facing communities.

He also highlighted the importance of integrating care for non-communicable diseases (NCDs), including other chronic conditions, into primary healthcare services so that patients can access essential prevention, screening, diagnosis and treatment closer to where they live.

“Evidence-based planning, sustainable financing and improving the quality of healthcare services are essential to building a health system that responds effectively to people’s needs,” Butera said.

His remarks come amid growing efforts across Africa to strengthen primary healthcare systems as countries face a rising burden of non-communicable diseases alongside persistent infectious disease challenges.

Conditions such as cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, cancer and chronic respiratory diseases require long-term care, regular monitoring and sustained investment in healthcare services.

Integrating these services into community-based primary healthcare can help reduce the need for patients to travel long distances to specialised facilities, improve early detection and ensure continuity of treatment.

Strengthening Africa’s health systems through data

The Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA) is a major continental platform convened by the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), bringing together policymakers, public health experts, researchers, development partners and other stakeholders to discuss Africa’s public health priorities.

The conference provides an opportunity to share research, exchange experiences and develop strategies for strengthening health systems, improving disease surveillance and advancing health security across the continent.

The 2026 discussions place particular importance on the role of reliable data, research and evidence in shaping public health policies and ensuring that limited resources are directed towards interventions with the greatest impact.

For African countries, improving the collection, analysis and use of health information is increasingly important in addressing gaps in healthcare access, strengthening accountability and making health financing more sustainable.

Butera’s participation highlights the importance of translating health data into practical decisions that improve service delivery, particularly at the primary healthcare level, where communities first access many essential health services.

Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK.

Find out how to listen to other BBC stations

World Service , · 28 Nov 2026 , · 23 mins

The Court of Arbitration for Sport has reinstated Senegal as Africa Cup of Nations champions, 10 months after one of the most controversial games in football history - and eight months after the Confederation of African Football overturned the result of the final and awarded the trophy to Morocco instead. But is this really the end of the story? More than the Score's John Bennett is joined by Senegalese journalist Babacar Diarra and North African football expert Maher Mezahi to discuss the decision, and the impact of the saga on the game in Africa. We also hear from former Premier League referee Graham Scott, who gives his take on the decisions that were made, as well as former Nigeria striker Daniel Amokachi. Unexpected questions and beyond the scoresheet chat. More than the Score tells stories from all over the world of sport. From Formula One to netball, MMA to figure skating, and Grand Slam tennis to Diamond League athletics. We've got interviews with extraordinary athletes, as well as the experts working behind the scenes, from football super-agents to the coaches keeping athletes in peak form. Plus, we've got the expertise of the BBC's top journalists, who share their insights from decades of covering sport at all levels. And if you've got your own take on the stories we cover, we'd love to hear from you. Email morethanthescore@bbc.co.uk, or WhatsApp us on 0044 800 032 0470. You can find more information, along with our privacy notice, on our website: www.bbcworldservice.com/morethanthescore

A Russian MiG-31 military jet (file photo)

Ukraine has said it damaged five Russian military aircraft in an attack on Russia's Savasleyka airfield, 300km (185 miles) east of Moscow.

Three MiG-31 and two Su-34s aircraft were hit, Kyiv's General Staff said, adding that the extent of the damage was still being assessed but that "there may be even better news to come". It did not elaborate on what weapons it had used to hit the airfield.

Russia has not commented on the strikes.

The airfield at Savasleyka, in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, has been a target for Ukraine for several years. It hosts aircraft used by Russia to launch hypersonic missiles and glide bombs.

The take-off of MiG-31s in particular frequently triggers nationwide alerts across Ukraine, as the Kinzhal missiles they carry have been known to hit large infrastructure and military targets and are difficult to shoot down.

Overnight, Kyiv also said it hit two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region some 800km (500 miles) from the front line – the latest in a series of long-range strikes which have dented Moscow's oil processing capacity.

"Did you repair them? We'll hit them again," the defence ministry in Kyiv said.

Samara region governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said the night-time attacks had been "a true ordeal", with more than 145 drones shot down. One person was killed and several towns experienced power outages, Fedorishchev said.

Kyiv also said it had hit a radar system as well as fuel and logistics depots across Ukrainian territories currently occupied by Russia.

"Without fuel, military vehicles cannot move; without ammunition, artillery falls silent," the defence ministry said, adding that every successful hit meant Moscow could carry out fewer strikes.

Kyiv has developed a thriving weapons industry and Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets well beyond the front line have become commonplace in the years since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.

On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin called for a tightening of security measures across the country's energy facilities.

But he also argued that Russia had managed to stabilise its domestic fuel market without suffering "critical damage" and added that Moscow would "inevitably" retaliate against Kyiv.

Ukraine continues to come under daily attack. Ten people were killed across several regions between 24 and 25 November, while thousands are without power after Russian strikes on energy infrastructure.

MN202611_d43pgxls27.t:
The sun shone on 2025's Thanksgiving Parade but the forecast this year is not so bright

Strong winds are threatening to disrupt Thursday's Thanksgiving parade in New York City for the first time since the Second World War.

A potent Nor'easter storm could impact the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade which is due to be taking place for the 100th time, with the risk that it could be too windy for the event's iconic balloons to fly.

The US National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning, valid from 10:00 local time (15:00 GMT) on Thursday until 01:00 (06:00 GMT) on Friday with gusts potentially reaching 60mph (97km/h) - although the very strongest winds are likely to occur after the parade is due to end.

Heavy rain and coastal flooding will pose additional hazards across the eastern USA as the storm sweeps through, while some inland parts could also see snow.

Western areas of the country have also faced Thanksgiving travel headaches, with Pacific storms and coastal flooding.

Storms targeting both US coasts threaten to snarl Thanksgiving travel for millions

The parade started life as the Macy's Christmas Parade, organised by employees at Macy's department store in New York City in a bid to boost holiday sales.

The first event took place on Thanksgiving Day 1924. It has only been cancelled during the Second World War, when it was put on hiatus between 1942 and 1944. As a result, this year marks the 100th parade.

It is due to take place from 08:30 local time (13:30 GMT), ending at around 12:00 (17:00 GMT) , and involves marching bands, street performers and floats parading through the streets of New York City, as well as 100 brightly-coloured inflatable balloons.

Confetti filled the air above this enormous turkey at the start of the 2025 parade

However, due to city regulations full-size balloons cannot fly if sustained winds exceed 23mph (37km/h), or in gusts of more than 35mph (56km/h).

There is a risk that Thursday will bring winds approaching those strengths.

However, record wind gusts also made the 1997 route a no-fly zone and the balloons were still featured in the parade.

The giant character balloons were tethered to golf carts that year.

In 1989, when a major snowstorm stopped balloon handlers getting to the parade route, the cheer and dance teams stepped in to pull the giant balloons along.

Over the last few days, a cluster of showers and thunderstorms has been swarming in the Gulf of Mexico.

That area of disturbed weather is now moving northwards, close to the east coast, and deepening into a potent area of low pressure - a Nor'easter storm, so called because it delivers strong north-easterly winds which drive into the east coast.

The National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning for New York City, as well as Long Island and north-east New Jersey.

It comes into force part-way through the parade and warns of strong to damaging wind gusts, which could affect trees and power lines and bring significant travel disruption.

The winds are forecast to strengthen through the day peaking during the evening, meaning the very strongest gusts are likely to hit after the parade is over. However, there is a risk that they could approach the threshold that would ground the balloons.

Up to 3in (75mm) of rain could fall with the risk of flooding, which could be exacerbated along the coast as high tides arrive on Thursday evening.

Large waves and high sea levels are expected, bringing the threat of erosion and damage along the shoreline.

Other eastern parts of the USA will also receive heavy rain and strong winds, with snow in some inland parts adding to the Thanksgiving travel headaches.

Bank of Kigali brought artists together with tax and legal experts to tackle the business side of creative careers, and committed to keep shaping BKreative around the realities creatives face.

Rwanda’s creative industry is growing fast. But behind every song, film and collection sits a business that must be managed, protected and financed. On Tuesday, 24 November, Bank of Kigali put that reality at the centre of the first BKreative Masterclass, held at the BK Arena Lounge with around 60 artists, creative entrepreneurs, managers and industry experts.

The afternoon opened with a keynote by Raoul Rugamba, Founder and CEO at Africa in Colors, who shared the lessons learned from building a career in Rwanda’s creative scene. What followed was a practical look at three areas that decide whether a creative career can last.

Bank of Kigali’s Taxation Unit unpacked how tax applies to creative work, from registering for a TIN to issuing EBM invoices, and showed how small gaps in compliance quietly cost creatives through withholding tax, missed contracts and penalties.

Music Producer, and the Co-founder of the Bionix, Christian Dessart, then turned to music contracts. He walked artists through the many revenue streams their work can generate, from authoring, publishing and distribution to performance and licensing, and how the foundation of generating those revenues start with negotiating the right contract.

The BKreative team closed the learning sessions with an overview of the bank’s financing solutions for creatives, along with a practical checklist to help them prepare before applying.

Artists raised their concerns about the financing gap and how the requirements are designed for more traditional businesses, and shared thoughts on how BKreative can be refined and enhanced. Many said that, alongside access to loans, they want to also be equipped with financial literacy, capacity building and more opportunities to showcase their talent.

That feedback speaks directly to what BKreative was built to do. Beyond financing, its mandate includes promoting financial literacy and connecting creatives to buyers and markets. The masterclass was a first step in delivering on that broader promise, and its format was deliberate: rather than bankers mainly speaking to artists, BKreative facilitated a conversation between creatives and experts from their own industry.

Bank of Kigali plans to build on this approach through future masterclasses and workshops, and through a BKreative podcast series that will bring industry experts and creatives into conversation and carry these discussions well beyond the room.

Building on the partnership introduced at the masterclass, BKreative in partnership with international legal experts, are subsidizing legal support to five Rwandan music artists with publishing, distribution or recording contracts with foreign companies in Africa, Europe, USA, and elsewhere. Selected artists will receive a contract review, mediation and negotiation with the company concerned, and follow-up until their case is resolved. Applications close on 15 December 2026.

The masterclass closed with remarks from Zaina Amri Sued, the Head of Sustainability from the BK Foundation, who said that “ Alongside financing, BK foundation also provides capacity building, in partnership with Bank of Kigali and with creatives themselves. What we want most is to keep these conversations going and to build solutions that fit the reality of creatives. This is a journey we want to continue together.

The Bkreative Masterclass was followed by a networking and a press conference announcing the BK 60 Concert, part of Bank of Kigali’s 60th anniversary celebrations.

MN202611_198bqg94mx3.t:
Watch: The CCTV that helped convict a Sydney policeman of double murder

It was just after 09:00 on a warm February morning when CCTV picked up a man dressed as an UberEats rider hovering on a sidewalk in one of Sydney's wealthiest neighbourhoods.

He dawdled for around 20 minutes, "steeling himself for what he was about to do" prosecutors say, before disappearing out of sight. Minutes later another CCTV camera captured the sound of gunshots ringing out.

Former police officer Beau Lamarre, 31, was on Wednesday found guilty of murdering his former partner Jesse Baird, a TV presenter, and Luke Davies, Baird's new partner, with his work-issued gun.

In February 2024, the bloodied belongings of Baird and Davies were found in a skip in the suburb of Cronulla, sparking a frantic search for the couple. It culminated in the discovery of their bodies on a rural property, partially buried beneath sticks and debris.

Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird had been dating only months when they were gunned down

During a two-month trial filled with at-times extraordinary testimony and a wealth of CCTV evidence, the court heard Lamarre had planned his crime over months.

Jurors watched CCTV of the then police officer purchasing a surfboard bag in which to put Baird's body, after casually sizing it up against a friend in the shop, and heard from a stream of former friends and colleagues who testified that Lamarre asked them for advice about everything from mobile phone signals to where he could buy a gun.

One recounted the chilling moment Lamarre told her that if he were ever to murder someone, he would leave their belongings in a dumpster and hide the body in bushland where they would never be found.

"What would you do if I told you I killed somebody? Would you help me hide the body?" he asked, according to her testimony.

Later, Lamarre asked for help in covering up the killings; his friends - none of whom have been implicated - say they began receiving panicked calls and odd requests from him.

One told the court Lamarre persuaded her to go for a drive in the country, during which he tried to dispose of the bodies at the family farm of a man he'd met on a dating app. Over the speakers, he played Taylor Swift's No Body, No Crime.

Baird, 26, and Lamarre - a one-time celebrity blogger who also had his own swimwear line on the side of his police work - met in a nightclub in October 2022. For Lamarre, it quickly became an infatuation, but for Baird, an AFL referee and former Network Ten presenter, the relationship appeared to be casual.

After discovering in April 2023 that Lamarre had gone through messages on his phone, and unfollowed other men on his Instagram account, Baird broke it off.

But Lamarre's obsession only grew. He watched Baird having sex with another man through his bedroom window, broke into his house multiple times, deleting contacts on his phone and turning on location settings so that he could engineer meetings with the TV presenter.

On one occasion Baird woke up to find Lamarre in his bedroom; not realising who it was, he chased him down the street. Lamarre was also convicted of aggravated break and enter over that incident on Wednesday.

Prosecutor Brett Hatfield said Baird was "oblivious to the accused's scheming and manipulations", and the pair briefly rekindled the relationship before Baird ended it definitively in November.

He'd discovered Lamarre had, again, been accessing his phone and had attempted to ward off a love rival by pretending to have received flowers from Baird.

Beau Lamarre pictured at the annual Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras parade in Sydney in 2020

His pride wounded, Hatfield said Lamarre's thoughts turned to a "darker place": "revenge".

He asked an old friend if her ex-partner could get him a gun: "This was the beginning of the plan for the murder," the prosecutor said.

In the months leading up to the killings, Lamarre bought a burner phone, a motorcycle helmet, and practised shooting in the woods. On holiday with a friend in Bali in January 2024 he tried to buy a silencer.

While his murder plans percolated, he also began lashing out with petty acts of malice, prosecutors said, such as putting water in the fuel tank of Baird's car.

But at the same time as he plotted, Lamarre was still trying to win his ex back.

On one occasion he pressured a friend to send Baird a 1,600-word message he had himself composed, claiming that he had cancer, and may need to have his arm amputated.

Under questioning in court, he said a naturopath he couldn't remember the name of had diagnosed him with "a form of sporadic cancer".

By the end of 2023, Baird had met and hit it off with Davies, 29. "It was early days but they were both smitten with each other," his mother, Helen Baird, told the court. He sent her a picture of the pair at a Pink concert. "I just sent a big love heart and said 'I'm so happy for both of you'."

Jesse Baird and Luke Davies at the Pink concert shortly before they were killed

Early on the morning of 19 February, Lamarre picked up a hire car he had asked his mother to rent and drove to Baird's home. After waiting several hours for Baird's housemates to leave, while disguised as an UberEats driver, he let himself in with a key he had copied.

Lamarre told the court he had been at Baird's home to pick up some belongings , including a A$25,000 (US$16,500, £12,600) Cartier ring, and had disguised himself to avoid the embarrassment of being recognised if anyone was home.

He claimed he let himself in when no one answered the door, and the two men were killed in separate struggles. He argued that Baird had been holding a knife and the first shot was fired to disarm him, and the second by accident. Davies shot himself when he grabbed the gun, Lamarre said.

But prosecutors told the jury Baird was shot in the back and then once again through his temple as he lay gravely wounded on the kitchen floor.

The evidence, Hatfield said, pointed to one thing only: "an execution".

Davies was then shot through a bedroom door as he tried to call emergency services. The court heard the panic in his voice as the seconds-long call was replayed before it dropped out.

After that, Lamarre set about trying to hide the evidence of what Hatfield called his "brazen and shocking murders".

One of his first actions was to call a friend. He testified Lamarre confessed he had "killed people" and asked him to take a day off work "to help him clean up his mess".

Later Lamarre pretended the call was a joke, saying, "Did you like my Oscar performance? Got you".

Meanwhile, Lamarre went to a DIY store to purchase mops, bleach and bin bags. After returning to Baird's house to clean up, he left the bodies wrapped in surfboard bags and tarpaulins in the courtyard.

Baird had been set to move out that week, and Lamarre used Baird's phone to reassure his housemates he had hired an Airtasker to move his belongings, adding, "I might be flying to Perth tonight".

Baird's housemates quickly spotted the surfboard bags when they returned home, snapping a photograph tendered in court which showed "red liquid" seeping out.

"I thought it was rusted water from the outdoor furniture," one of the women said.

The surfboard bags were gone the next morning.

Lamarre was captured on CCTV sizing up a surfboard bag in the days before the murders

Lamarre had hired a van, and over the next two days made more trips to the DIY store and a sports shop to buy gumboots, a wheelbarrow, bigger surfboard bags and 10kg weights. He squeezed in a hospital appointment for a minor procedure and paused for a sushi date with a friend, CCTV showing him laughing and eating as the bodies lay in the back of his van.

On 21 February, he picked up another friend in the van for what she thought was lunch.

There were blue tarps in the back and it smelled "lemony", she told the court. She "wasn't allowed to put the windows up or turn the aircon off" as they motored towards Goulburn, 200km southwest of Sydney, stopping only at another DIY store, where he asked her to buy an angle grinder.

His friend told the court she remembers Lamarre playing No Body, No Crime at some point: "It's a very niche song."

Arriving at a farm owned by a Hinge date's family, Lamarre used the angle grinder to cut through a padlock, making his way to a dam where he unsuccessfully tried to sink the bodies.

It was now late at night and he drove his friend, by this time upset and confused, home before returning to retrieve the bodies. He then left them in the van, parked in Sydney overnight, before driving once more to Goulburn, where he dumped the bodies near a monastery.

Later that day he visited another friend, telling her to look up the definition of schizophrenia and asking whether he could use her hose, because "there was a bit of blood he had to scrub off" the hired van, the court heard.

The deaths of Baird and Davies triggered an outpouring of horror in Sydney

By this time police were closing in, and on 23 February Lamarre went to turn himself in at Bondi police station. On the way, he called a police helpline.

"I've been bullied by multiple New South Wales police force members," he told the woman on the other end of the line. "All this stress and trauma and psychological abuse and trauma - did I say trauma already? - has caused me to not sleep, get anxious, it's caused me to have some symptoms of schizophrenia."

"Actually sorry, you know what, can you just... delete that whole thing. We'll just keep it short and sweet."

He wasn't sure when he'd be back to work, he said. Shortly afterwards he was arrested and charged with murder , and the bodies of Baird and Davies were found four days later.

Lamarre's lawyer John Stratton insisted he'd acted in self-defence and had "panicked" realising how the scene would look to outsiders.

The former police officer did plenty of "foolish" and "unusual" things - "He was, it's fair to say, a poorly behaved boyfriend," Stratton said - but that did not make him a murderer.

Ultimately, however, the jury was not convinced and took just over an hour to convict him. He will be sentenced in March and faces life in prison.

MN202611_1um3q1qwmik.t:
Big technology firms connected to AI continued seeing their shares fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading.

All three main US stock market indices were down, with the tech-dominated Nasdaq shedding almost 4%.

The declines come amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment which has rattled investors in recent weeks.

Shares in other major tech firms, including Amazon, Tesla and SpaceX, Micrsoft and Meta were also down.

The US government also announced a raft of new tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy.

The value of big tech companies have sheltered the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, but share prices in recent weeks have been volatile in response to the US midterm elections and other events in the AI industry.

The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang after revelations of his extra marital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly.

Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact.

Investors have taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms and even a moratorium on the development of new data centres.

Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will eventually pay off.

Investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, which said the technology will remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.

MN202611_5eu59bn1q5.t:
Nearly seven tonnes of chemicals used to manufacture meth as well as industrial equipment were also seized

Five Mexican nationals and a Nigerian businessman have been arrested in Nigeria after authorities uncovered an industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratory, the country's drug enforcement agency says.

More than 1.5 tonnes of the highly addictive synthetic drug, commonly known as meth, was seized from the facility in the south-eastern state of Enugu. The haul included both finished drugs and meth still being produced.

The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) estimates the drugs are worth $227m (£173m).

It is the fourth industrial-scale meth laboratory with alleged links to Mexican drug cartels to have been discovered in Nigeria in recent months.

Earlier this year, Nigerian authorities uncovered similar laboratories in Ogun, Oyo and Ebonyi states

The Nigerian businessman, 63-year-old Chuks Enoch Ezeike, also known as "Over Size", is accused of setting up the laboratory and smuggling the five Mexicans into the country using forged Argentine, Colombian and Chilean passports.

The NDLEA identified the five as Oscar Ramos-Cardenas, who it described as the alleged leader of the group, Juan Antonio Sarabia-Cabrera, Luis Enrique Garcia-Amador, Jose Alejandro Renteria-Reyes and Salomon Cabanillas-Torres.

The laboratory, situated behind an oil company in Enugu, also had accommodation for the Mexican nationals, allowing them to live and work there without attracting attention, the agency said.

Speaking at a news conference in the capital, Abuja, on Wednesday, NDLEA chief Mohamed Buba Marwa said the arrests followed a seven-month investigation involving several countries.

The agency had been monitoring Ezeike since April, when it received intelligence allegedly linking him to Ramos-Cardenas, a Mexican national suspected of specialising in large-scale meth production.

In August, the five Mexicans were refused entry into Nigeria after arriving at Abuja's international airport and were sent back to Mexico.

But less than a month later, they tried again, travelling through Colombia and France before arriving in neighbouring Benin, where they were allegedly given forged passports.

This time, Nigerian authorities deliberately allowed them into the country, Marwa said.

"We wanted the whole network: the meth specialist, the financier, the factory and the product. Sending them home a second time would only have postponed the problem," he said.

The men were allegedly met by Ezeike in Lagos before being taken to Enugu, where they were kept under surveillance.

More than 200 anti-narcotics officers were deployed on 11 November to raid the laboratory and a hotel where Ezeike was staying in simultaneous operations.

The five Mexicans were arrested while producing the drug, the agency said. Ezeike told investigators they had been due to leave Nigeria two days later.

Nearly seven tonnes of chemicals used to manufacture meth, as well as industrial equipment, were also seized.

The arrests come amid growing concerns about Mexican drug cartels setting up production bases in West Africa

The NDLEA said Ezeike had admitted owning the laboratory and bringing the Mexican nationals into Nigeria to produce the drug.

Investigators believe the operation was part of a wider international criminal network in which a Mexican cartel recruited and paid specialists to manufacture meth, while Nigerian collaborators allegedly provided the facilities and resources.

The agency has not identified the Mexican cartel it suspects was involved or said whether the six suspects have been formally charged.

The arrests come amid growing concerns about Mexican drug cartels setting up production bases in West Africa, a region long used as a transit route for illicit drugs.

While some of the meth produced in the region supplies a growing local market, traffickers also target lucrative overseas markets, particularly in Europe and Asia.

Earlier this year, Nigerian authorities uncovered similar laboratories in Ogun, Oyo and Ebonyi states.

The latest operation brings to 10 the number of suspected Mexican meth production specialists arrested in Nigeria in recent months, according to the NDLEA. Five others arrested in earlier operations are already in custody awaiting trial.

Issuing a warning to foreign drug cartels, Marwa said: "Nigeria is not your laboratory. It is not your warehouse, and it is not your transit route."

MN202611_j55twayqd4.t:
Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting 11,000 jobs at risk, after its owners failed to find a buyer to keep it in business.

The discount retailer formally entered administration on Wednesday afternoon, just weeks before Christmas.

Poundland's American owners held talks with several bidders over a last-minute rescue deal for the business, but no transaction was reached.

This led to Poundland's boss filing for administration, with consultancy Alix Partners appointed to oversee the process.

Alix Partners will pursue a sale of the business and its assets, with Poundland likely to be broken up, for example with some of its stores sold off to rival retailers.

Poundland is facing collapse - what's gone wrong?

Previously US-based owner Gordon Brothers was criticised over how it had handled the Poundland sale process, with insiders saying it was driving a viable business into the ground to make money through insolvency.

But the investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, had denied the claim.

Gordon Brothers had stated Poundland was "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".

But this was in stark contrast to Poundland's boss Barry Williams, who had said the business was making a "strong recovery".

One of the central stumbling blocks in negotiations to keep the business afloat was a shareholder loan Gordon Brothers inherited when it bought the business for less than £1 last year.

Gordon Brothers was owed £22.5m of that loan, while the previous owner Pepco was owed £7.5m.

Gordon Brothers rejected various offers to buy the business as a going concern with deals to pay off that loan.

Irish firm Martin Property Group offered to pay off £5m of the loan up front, and defer the rest of the payments to 2030. This was rejected.

Gordon Brothers also rejected a deal from the London-based Xyra group, which offered £12.5m up front but ran out of time to get a deal over the line.

A German investment firm, Zachert Private Equity, is also understood to have made a late offer, but that too was rejected.

The crisis at Poundland really came to a head over the past few weeks after Gordon Brothers restricted access to some funds for day-to-day operations.

This meant that stock at the retailer was not being replenished at the necessary pace in the vital run-up to the festive period.

On the funding question, Gordon Brothers said it had put £85m into the firm over a year to help save it from insolvency.

MN202611_d7df286bj2.t:
A Canadian astronaut aboard the International Space Station is celebrating the birth of his third child from hundreds of miles above Earth.

Joshua Kutryk and his wife, Heather Kutryk, welcomed their daughter as the astronaut takes part in a six-month space mission that began in October, the Canadian Space Agency announced on Tuesday.

"Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our new little star into our lives," said the couple in a statement shared by the agency.

Joshua Kutryk, currently on his first space mission, is just the fourth astronaut in history to miss the birth of a child while aboard the International Space Station.

The couple have two older children, aged five and seven.

"We are very proud of our growing family and are looking forward to getting our little crew of five all reunited."

In a statement, the couple said that Joshua's spaceflight was a "childhood dream" come true.

"We hope to show our children that big dreams are worth pursuing, that hard work and determination matter, and that with the support of family and a strong community, extraordinary things are possible," they said.

Prior to becoming an astronaut, Kutryk, from Fort Saskatchewan, Alberta, was a fighter pilot and a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force. He was recruited by the Canadian Space Agency in 2017.

Heather Kutryk said her family had been preparing for years prior to her husband's missing, calling it "a long time coming"

Kutryk was the only Canadian selected to be part of NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission, where four astronauts are conducting scientific experiments and testing new technologies in space.

The crew also includes two US astronauts, Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins, and one Russian astronaut, Sergey Teteryatnikov.

Before their take off on 1 October, Heather Kutryk told Canada's public broadcaster CBC News that her family had been preparing for years before the mission, saying it was "a long time coming".

Heather added that her pregnancy was "not exactly planned" but that it was "a great thing".

"I'm not that stressed out. I feel like we have a really good community. I feel well supported by both CSA and Nasa," she said.

"It's six months, I feel like we'll be fine."

In a separate interview with BBC's US news partner CBS News, Joshua Kutryk said he hopes his new child will look at his dad's mission as "making some sacrifice, taking some risk, but doing so in the name of public service and the name, in my case, for Canada."

KIGALI – African economies continue to export raw materials for processing elsewhere, while African professionals contribute to technologies whose ownership and commercial returns raise questions about how much value the continent captures.

Leaders say the continent’s economic transformation will depend not only on what the continent produces, but also on how much value it retains from its own resources, skills and ideas.

Changing that pattern has emerged as a strong challenge for African countries seeking to build stronger industries, develop homegrown technologies and reduce dependence on external expertise.

The United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) estimates that manufacturing accounted for 10.6 per cent of Africa’s GDP in 2024, compared with a global average of 16.5 per cent. Manufacturing value added per person stood at just US$212, against a global average of US$1,937.

This persistent gap in the continent’s capacity to turn its resources into higher-value products featured prominently during a generational exchange at the eighth YouthConnekt Africa Summit in Kigali on Wednesday, November 25, 2026.

President Paul Kagame, Lesotho Prime Minister Samuel Ntsokoane Matekane and Gabon’s Vice-President Hugues Alexandre Barro Chambrier discussed the economic transformation they want young Africans to drive.

Barro illustrated the challenge through Gabon’s efforts to diversify its economy and expand local processing of natural resources.

He said the country was reforming its training system to prepare young people for sectors where it has comparative advantages, while equipping them with skills in emerging fields such as artificial intelligence.

But he argued that developing skills would have limited economic impact if African countries continued exporting resources without capturing the value created through processing.

“We can no longer remain producers of timber, only for those resources to be processed abroad and then imported back to our countries. That makes no economic sense. Processing resources locally would create opportunities including jobs in manufacturing and technical services,” he said.

He made a similar argument about manganese, calling for more local processing and stronger trade among African countries to improve their competitiveness in international markets.

An OECD analysis of critical minerals in Africa found that 24 per cent of the continent’s critical mineral exports were shipped in raw form, while a further 72 per cent were semi-processed. This means that even where some processing takes place, much of the higher-value industrial activity remains outside the continent.

Barro said training must therefore respond to the needs of African economies, pointing to cooperation with Rwanda, where Gabonese students are pursuing specialized studies, as one way of building relevant skills within the continent.

From Supplying Talent to Creating Technology

Kagame extended the argument to the technology industry, where he said Africa risks contributing talent without taking a sufficiently strong position in developing and owning the technologies shaping the future.

He noted that many companies behind the world’s most advanced technologies already employ Africans, including engineers, data analysts and innovators.

The continent, he argued, has human capability that could support technological development. What remains is to create the conditions that allow that expertise to produce technologies suited to African economies.

Africa accounts for only about 0.6 per cent of global data-centre capacity, according to the Africa Data Centres Association’s 2026 report. These facilities provide the computing and storage infrastructure needed for cloud services and increasingly sophisticated artificial intelligence applications.

Their limited availability constrains the continent’s ability to build and operate more of its own digital services. “We should not talk about technology as though it belongs elsewhere and only comes to us because we have requested or begged for access to it,” Kagame said.

The aim, he said, should be to develop technologies that address African needs in areas such as medicine, agriculture and transport, rather than remain dependent on solutions developed elsewhere.

“We cannot continue being junior partners in everything. At some point, we must become equal partners. Partnerships with international technology companies must be based on equality, with African countries taking a stronger role in shaping technological development,” Kagame noted.

According to him, AI offers opportunities to improve productivity across several sectors but its rapid development also brings risks, particularly concerning safety and privacy. African countries must therefore build the capacity to manage those risks alongside the benefits.

The discussion also touched on Africa’s wider relationship with the rest of the world, with Kagame insisting that the continent must move away from depending on external generosity and seeking approval elsewhere for its achievements.

He said African success should be recognized on the strength of the continent’s own efforts and ability to work together, rather than depend on validation from outside.

“We have been in that position for too long. It is painful to see that African success and the recognition of Africa’s rightful place in the world often seem to require validation from somebody else,” he said.

Matekane shared the view that Africa has the resources to sustain itself, challenging young entrepreneurs to use the continent’s opportunities for their own benefit and that of Africa as a whole.

“Even those who come from outside the continent do so because Africa has something they need, something they may not have in their own countries,” he said.

He called for fewer barriers to business across African borders, including making it easier for companies to move workers and operate in other countries. Consensus was built around stronger regional markets, lower poverty and greater mobility across the continent.

Trade between African countries reached an estimated US$206.6 billion in 2024, but represented only 15.3 per cent of the continent’s total trade, according to Afreximbank.

That leaves considerable scope for African economies to strengthen regional supply chains and create larger markets for goods produced within the continent.

MN202611_z566uuy49g.t:
Leny Yoro will be available for Manchester United's game against Brentford on Saturday after his one-match ban was rescinded

Leny Yoro's overturned red card against Liverpool appears to have turned into an unseemly difference of opinion between Manchester United and referees' body Pro Ref.

Yoro was sent off after bringing down Liverpool striker Alexander Isak in the eighth minute of the 4-0 defeat at Anfield.

Referee Sam Barrott sent off the France international, and the decision was backed up by video assistant referee (VAR) John Brooks.

It split opinion among pundits and fans. Would Isak have got to the ball before goalkeeper Senne Lammens? Was it really a clear goalscoring chance?

First, a Football Association regulatory commission upheld United's appeal and cancelled the red card.

Then Pro Ref boss Howard Webb said the red card was not "clearly wrong" - just moments before United held a pre-match news conference.

Over to Red Devils head coach Mauricio Pochettino, who was fiercely critical of the decision, and in particular the VAR.

But how can Pro Ref still believe the decision was right when an FA commission said it was wrong?

BBC Sport looks at how the system works.

So United won their appeal. Pro Ref would disagree. Could the two sides not just agree to differ?

"You ask me a question and I need to defend our situation and our club and our players," Pochettino said about Yoro's red card.

It continued a theme from his post-match news conference.

You can see why Pochettino would be keen to talk about the red card, rather than the performance of his players. After all, United had just lost the first game of his tenure. Was the Argentine keen to create a siege mentality?

You can also understand United's frustration - two of their biggest games of the season so far have been defined by refereeing decisions.

The first was the VAR error to allow Erling Haaland's match-winning goal in the Manchester derby, when Enzo Fernandez clearly committed an offside offence.

As for the Yoro incident, Pochettino reserved much his criticism for the VAR. United felt he only took a cursory look at where the ball would run.

It should be noted that Match Officials Mic'd up, on which Webb gave his views, was filmed on Monday evening - before the result of the appeal.

Would that change his opinion? Almost certainly not.

Webb acknowledged the argument against a red card, which was Isak would not get the ball. But he was adamant it was not such an egregious error that it required a VAR intervention.

So are we back to arguing about when VAR should get involved?

The VAR threshold is too high, until it is too low. Rinse and repeat.

It is the Premier League clubs, and not Pro Ref nor the FA, who set where the bar sits.

Take the last stakeholders' survey, which helps to shape how the game is officiated.

It found 65% wanted to maintain the current threshold for VAR intervention, 20% to increase it, and just 15% to lower it.

But, of course, where the Yoro incident sits is still a matter of opinion.

'And the three points?' - Pochettino after Yoro red overturned

How confusing it must be for a supporter just watching on, hoping to understand.

An FA regulatory commission has said the red card decision was wrong. Case closed? Not so fast.

Pro Ref will not always agree with the decision of an appeal board, nor will they use it as a barometer for future decisions.

And the burden of proof for a VAR intervention is considered higher than for an FA commission.

Pro Ref places far more stock upon the judgements of the Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel.

The KMI Panel creates the merit table for referees, and helps shape how decisions are made in the future - especially for the VARs.

But surely the FA is the higher body? Not quite.

The FA is responsible purely for disciplinary measures and has no say on how games at the professional level are refereed.

If the Premier League tells Pro Ref the decision is right or wrong, that counts far more than any vote by an FA commission.

BBC Sport understands the club argued that if Isak had maintained his top recorded speed, he would not have got to the ball first.

The club say that is objectively provable, within minutes, using data. This, they say, was not a subjective decision.

To argue it was not subjective goes completely against the nature of the decision - it required a referee's judgement.

Whatever this data was, it most definitely was not available to the referees. The VAR cannot call upon a 3D animation of each player, detailing their running speed and providing an objective result.

How much stock did the commission place on this evidence? We will not know until the written reasons are published in a few days' time.

But United are not going to let this lie, and Pro Ref is not going to bend.

Such is the way FA commissions work, you can never be sure who will win.

There are three panel members who are usually former players, but occasionally you might get a retired referee.

The role of the commission is not to "usurp the referee by re-refereeing the incident".

A designated referee delegate is present to answer questions on the laws of the game, but they cannot offer an opinion on the incident.

The only input Pro Ref has is the official's report - a short entry by the referee that says which law was used for the red card. There is no other context.

It will read something like this: "I have to report that I, as the referee, sent off Yoro, Leny of Manchester United FC Under Law 12 section: S5."

The burden is on the club to prove its case by submitting a body of evidence - videos, images and testimony.

There is no right of reply. The evidence is weighed up by the panel, a vote is cast and the majority wins.

It makes predicting the outcome notoriously difficult, as the system is an opinion poll based upon a club trying to persuade at least two people to agree with them.

Take a look at Aston Villa 's successful appeal against Douglas Luiz's red card for violent conduct four years ago. Luiz had been sent off via a VAR review for a headbutt on Aleksandar Mitrovic.

The panel's written reasons stated the appeal was won partly because Luiz was "a few inches shorter than Mr Mitrovic so his forehead is naturally at the same height as Mr Mitrovic's nose/face as the two players come together".

So, when the two players bumped chests the headbutt was just an accident. Appeal upheld because Luiz was a bit shorter.

Some might think anything is worth trying.

TV chef Gordon Ramsay is to lead the new presenting line-up on BBC motoring show Top Gear, which is being revived four years after it was last on air.

Ramsay will take the driving seat alongside as yet unnamed co-presenters when the show starts filming next year. It will return to screens in 2028.

The long-running programme has been off air since 2022, when co-host Andrew Flintoff suffered serious facial and rib injuries after his open-topped three-wheeled car overturned at the show's test-track.

In a statement announcing his new role, Ramsay said he wants to bring "a fresh energy and ambition" to the show's formula of being "surprising, entertaining and [with] just the right amount of chaos".

MN202611_wbgqk7g4a.t:
Bellingham finished 11th in the 2026 Ballon d'Or

Is there a better central midfielder on the planet than Jude Bellingham right now?

Not according to Jose Mourinho. The Real Madrid manager might be trying to manage the Englishman's minutes, but he did not hold back in his praise after the 23-year-old came off the bench and scored a superb volley , helping Real overturn a half-time deficit to beat PSV Eindhoven 5-1.

"He has physicality, he has technique, he has tactical understanding of the game, he has ambition, he has absolutely everything," Mourinho said.

"He's an absolutely extraordinary player and for me, without any doubt, the best midfielder in the world."

Bellingham's impressive 45-minute cameo came just nine days after an outstanding, all-action display for England in a 3-2 Nations League win in Spain.

While the former Birmingham and Borussia Dortmund player also earned plenty of plaudits for his displays at the 2026 World Cup, where he scored seven times, Mourinho believes Bellingham's unique blend of craft and graft isn't yet fully appreciated.

"He can play as a '10', as an '8', with two pivots, with one," Mourinho said after the win against PSV. "That's why I said, when the Ballon d'Or was discussed, that it was outrageous he wasn't among the top 10."

While wingers like Lamine Yamal or Michael Olise are also likely to be contenders for the 2027 award, is there anyone you would rather have in central midfield than Bellingham?

BBC Sport looks at what makes him so good, and who his closest challengers are.

Although only 23, Bellingham is already in his fourth year at Real Madrid and is on course for his most productive campaign since his debut season in 2023-24, when he scored 23 goals and provided 13 assists, including setting up Vinicius Jr in the Champions League final.

He has seven goals and four assists in 18 appearances this season. Only three central midfielders have more goal involvements across Europe's top five leagues, but Bellingham's all-round game is what sets him apart.

He leads his Real team-mates for possession won, duels won and fouls won. And while only Kylian Mbappe has had more shots on target, Bellingham offers far more than just late runs into the box.

He has played more passes into the final third than any other Real player, leads the club for ball carries and is second only to Arda Guler for chances created.

When Bellingham's coaches at Birmingham gave him the number 22 shirt, it reflected their belief that he could play any role, as a number 10, 8 or 4.

He has fulfilled that potential to become the complete midfielder.

While Bellingham made his senior debut with Birmingham, Vitinha also spent part of his formative years in the Midlands, scoring once in 22 appearances during a loan spell at Wolves - a spectacular long-range strike against Chorley in 2021.

But goalscoring isn't what the Portuguese playmaker is best known for - it is his metronomic passing.

The 26-year-old has played a pivotal role in Paris St-Germain's back-to-back Champions League triumphs, with manager Luis Enrique saying he "embodies the perfect midfielder".

He was named man of the match in the victory over Arsenal last season, having completed 141 of his 150 passes, matching the Champions League final record set by Barcelona's Xavi in 2011.

Vitinha finished third in the Ballon d'Or voting in 2025 but slipped to 14th this year, a ranking Luis Enrique disagreed with.

"It's a real pleasure to have a player with such physical abilities and that mentality," the PSG boss said last month. "He's at an incredible level."

Rice finished one place below Vitinha, and four below England team-mate Bellingham, in the 2026 Ballon d'Or rankings after helping Arsenal win their first Premier League title since 2004.

He briefly played at centre-back as a youngster at West Ham before establishing himself as a top-class defensive midfielder for the Hammers. But since joining the Gunners in 2023 he has taken his game to another level, adding significantly more attacking output.

Rice created 17 big chances in the Premier League last season, as defined by Opta, a total bettered only by Bruno Fernandes and Rayan Cherki.

The 27-year-old has also registered 14 assists in all club competitions since August 2025. While set-pieces have undoubtedly contributed to that tally, he offers much more.

He ranks among the top 4% of central midfielders across Europe's top five leagues for progressive carries, while posting similarly impressive figures for chances created, touches and expected assists.

The 2024 Ballon d'Or winner missed Spain's Nations League defeat by England this month through injury, and his absence was keenly felt as the hosts uncharacteristically struggled for control, at least against 11 men.

It was a far cry from Spain's triumphant Euro 2024 and 2026 World Cup campaigns, both of which ended with him being named player of the tournament.

The 30-year-old completed 756 passes as Spain won their second global title, the highest total ever recorded at a World Cup.

His performances this summer were all the more impressive given that he had taken time to return to his best after tearing his anterior cruciate ligament, an injury that sidelined him for most of the 2024-25 campaign.

The former Manchester City player has slotted in seamlessly since joining Barcelona in August, and averages 106 successful passes per 90 minutes in La Liga - the second-highest figure, behind Vitinha, of any player in the top five European leagues.

The student playing in La Liga: Introvert Rodri's unique rise to top

Pedri may be six years younger than Rodri, his midfield partner at the Camp Nou, but he boasts extraordinary experience for a 24-year-old, having made more than 250 appearances for Barcelona, not to mention playing at two European Championships and two World Cups.

The Tenerife-born midfielder combines tigerish work-rate with quality in possession.

He has created 26 chances from open play in La Liga this season, the sixth-highest total across Europe's top five leagues, and wins possession an average of 7.6 times per 90 minutes, the 10th-highest figure.

However, such is Spain's wealth of midfield options that he is not even guaranteed a starting place for his country, with Fabian Ruiz preferred for their final three matches at the 2026 World Cup.

Paris St-Germain midfielder Ruiz, who finished 10th in this year's Ballon d'Or rankings, also deserves to be in any debate about the world's best midfielders.

He might not yet have the profile of Barcelona team-mates Rodri or Pedri, but on current form alone, versatile youngster Lopez is one of Europe's best box-to-box goalscorers.

The 23-year-old already has nine goals and seven assists this season. Counting only goals scored in Europe's top five leagues and the Champions League, no central midfielder has more.

While Lopez can also operate on the wing, the presence of Lamine Yamal and Anthony Gordon means he has mainly featured as a number eight or a number 10 this term.

The Barcelona academy graduate played only a bit-part role as Spain won Euro 2024 and was unfortunate to miss the World Cup after breaking a bone in his foot in May.

However, a summer off enabled him to hit the ground running this season, and he has not looked back.
