MN202611_17urczqjaec.t:
King Power, the Thai business that Khun Aiyawatt 'Top' Srivaddhanaprabha is part of, bought Leicester for £35m in 2010

Leicester City owner Khun Aiyawatt 'Top' Srivaddhanaprabha has confirmed the one-time Premier League title winners are no longer up for sale and there will be a "refocus" on rebuilding the side after years of decline.

The Foxes were put on the market in the summer after back-to-back relegations saw the side drop from the Premier League and straight through the Championship to land in England's third tier for just the second time in the club's 142-year history.

A sales brochure was produced by US investment bank Citigroup in which an asking price of more than £200m was put on a League One club that a decade ago had defied all expectations by winning the Premier League title at 5,000-1 odds.

Leicester never publicly acknowledged that the club had been put up for sale, with under-fire chief football officer Jon Rudkin going so far as to say he "cannot comment on speculation" when asked about it in a rare interview with BBC Radio Leicester in October.

Khun Top, however, has now said that there were no takers when investment had been sought for a side that the Srivaddhanaprabha family, through its King Power duty free business in Thailand, have owned for 16 years.

"We recently undertook a structured process to explore whether new investment or a change of ownership could actually be the right thing for the club," Khun Top wrote in an open letter to Leicester City supporters on the club's website. , external

"Those discussions have not resulted in an agreement, and I have decided to conclude the process to enable us to refocus on the work needed to move the club forward."

'Business as always' - Foxes boss Martin brushes off sales talk

Listen to BBC Radio Leicester's When You're Smiling podcast

Pre-match, post-match and topical Foxes content

Three relegations in four years, having yo-yoed between the Premier League and Championship before going down to League One, has badly damaged the relationship between the Foxes' owners and their supporter base.

While a golden age of success was bankrolled by King Power, with Premier League glory in 2016 followed up by FA Cup success in 2021, high spending on an underperforming side in recent years has led to an increasing number of supporters calling for Khun Top to sell up.

But the Thai businessman said he has a "deep connection" to Leicester and "its people".

And it is not just euphoric sporting moments that have forged the bond he is talking about, as his father - and predecessor as Foxes chairman - Khun Vichai died in a helicopter crash outside the stadium in 2018.

"For my family and me, Leicester City has been a big part of our lives for many years," he said.

"We have experienced extraordinary moments together, as well as some very difficult ones."

Khun Top added that the struggles of recent years, which included the club being hit with a points penalty last season for breaking spending rules, has got him "thinking a lot about our direction".

Earlier this year he told BBC Radio Leicester that he shoulders the blame for the club's decline.

"Making better decisions" as well as "continuing to learn from our past experiences" are two steps the club "need to take", he said.

Khun Top has insisted that through King Power, a company that has endured difficulties in recent years, the club's "financial position remains secure".

However, he added that there was "work needed to put Leicester City on a more sustainable footing".

"That has been a principle behind the work and decisions of the last year – giving the club the appropriate support for its immediate circumstances, while building the organisational discipline and financial resilience that will underpin a responsible plan for future growth," he said.

As part of Khun Top's missive, he confirmed that chief executive Kevin Davies will be stepping down from the role in December.

Davies had only been in the job since March, and was promoted to the position after a shake-up of a number of leadership roles.

MN202611_10j1ljjtiy5.t:
Senegal's football federation reacted to the Cas verdict on social media with a picture of the side lifting the Afcon trophy alongside the caption "again and always champions of Africa"

That was the initial reaction of Senegal football federation (FSF) president Abdoulaye Fall to the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) to reinstate the West Africans as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations champions.

The Teranga Lions beat Morocco 1-0 in January's final but were stripped of the title in March by a Confederation of African Football (Caf) appeals board, which imposed a 3-0 forfeit after they walked off the pitch in protest at a penalty awarded against them when the game was goalless.

Following a hearing in Lausanne in October, a three-man Cas panel unanimously overturned that ruling by Caf, effectively judging that the decisions taken by referee Jean-Jacques Ndala in restarting the match and playing it to a conclusion were final.

Morocco's football federation (FRMF), however, says it will "pursue all available legal avenues to challenge the decision".

The North Africans could yet take their fight to the Swiss Federal Court.

Those in Senegal have celebrated the return of the title, while several legal experts have backed the Cas verdict.

Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 winners by court ruling

Senegal's talisman Sadio Mane, who was named player of the tournament at Afcon 2025, said the ruling "fills us with joy".

The 34-year-old former Liverpool man thanked his team-mates and Senegal staff as well as the whole Senegalese nation at home and abroad.

"Your faith in us gave us strength during the most difficult moments. This victory is yours, too," he said in a statement on social media.

Senegal captain Kalidou Koulibaly, who missed the final through injury, echoed that sentiment.

"Some victories are won on the pitch, while others are won in the heart of a people," he said in a post on Facebook.

"Long before this verdict, there was you - your prayers, your flags in the windows, your fervour, and the pride that unites us all: the pride of the people of Teranga."

Pape Gueye, the man who scored the extra-time winner in Rabat, described the Cas decision as "an immense relief".

Both he and Mane had a message of support for Morocco.

"Senegal and Morocco are brotherly nations; may our shared passion for football continue to bring us closer together," Mane said.

Gueye added: "Beyond football, the respect and fraternity between our two peoples remain what matters most. Let's hold on to that.

Afcon: Is the Senegal v Morocco saga finally over?

Morocco's main complaint is that Articles 82 and 84 of Afcon tournament regulations - which were implemented by the Caf appeals board in March - were not followed by Cas.

Article 82 states that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" it shall be "considered [the loser] and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition".

Article 84 then states a 3-0 forfeit should be imposed on a team which is eliminated in such circumstances.

"There [are] football rules that should have been applied by the referee," former Morocco international Hassan Kachloul told BBC Sport.

"When the Senegalese players left the pitch, the game should have been over."

The FRMF registered its "surprise" at the Cas decision and said that the panel "failed to account for the stance recently established" by the International Football Association Board (Ifab), the game's ultimate lawmakers, and world governing body Fifa regarding players leaving the field of play without the referee's permission.

However, Ifab only updated its laws in April - three months after the Afcon final - to state that a referee may send off any player who leaves the field when protesting a decision.

Moroccan football journalist Jalal Bounouar says his compatriots are "frustrated and disappointed" by the ruling.

"The main reason is that Caf's appeal board had already applied Article 82 and 84 of the competition regulations which considered Senegal to have forfeited the match," he told Newsday on the BBC World Service.

"Many Moroccans feel the decision by Cas has ignored the importance of these rules. From the Moroccan perspective, the referee should have taken stronger disciplinary action.

"We feel that our team was put in a difficult situation and that the final was not managed fairly."

Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 champions - ten months on

Cas has a long-standing practice of following what has been called the 'field of play' doctrine.

It refrains from "reviewing decisions taken on the playing field by referees for applying the rules of the game, unless there is evidence that those rules were applied arbitrarily or in bad faith".

"The primary argument was that the referee is the master of the decision on the pitch," said Serge Vittoz, a member of the FSF's legal team.

Raymond Hack, both a former head of disciplinary at Caf and a former arbiter at Cas, said the judgement was the "correct verdict".

"What everyone seems to forget - and whilst there may be contradictory information in Article 82 and 84 - decisions taken by the referee during the match are final," the South African told the BBC World Service.

"Only the referee can start a game. Only a referee can end a game."

For former Nigeria striker Daniel Amokachi, an Afcon winner in 1994, the Cas ruling is "the right decision".

"At the end of the day, the man in charge of the match (Ndala) restarted the game, the game ended," he said.

Caf president Patrice Motsepe has repeatedly said his organisation will respect and adhere to Cas' decision

Caf has already tightened its own regulations to avoid a repeat.

But Algerian sports journalist Maher Mezahi says the continental governing body still needs to salvage its image.

"How many times have we seen Caf's legal institutions, whether it be the disciplinary board or the appeals committee, come up with these decisions that we all find ridiculous," he said.

"They end up being challenged at Cas and eventually they get overturned.

"We have to rebuild trust in Caf's own judicial bodies because it is a little bit humiliating and degrading and it brings the entire reputation of the confederation into disrepute."

The 2027 Afcon is scheduled to take place in June and July next year, and Senegal and Morocco were among the first qualifiers earlier this month.

Kachloul says the next tournament provides a chance to draw a definitive line under what happened in Rabat in January.

"This event, wherever you look at it on the Senegalese side or Moroccan side, doesn't look good at all," the one-time Aston Villa midfielder said.

"They are lucky to have another [Afcon] tournament in six months to redeem themselves and to paint a better picture of African football.

"The best way to prove that you're the best is to go back on the pitch and let the football talk."

MN202611_1j1v88ko4pe.t:
Ahavuye isanamu, Uganda People's Defence Force (UPDF)

Reta ya Repuburika ya Demokarasi ya Kongo (RDC) yasavye Uganda gusigura ubutumwa umukuru w'igisirikare c'ico gihugu Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba aherutse gucisha kuri konte yiwe y'urubuga rwa X, ku ntambara irangwa mu buseruko bwa RDC.

Muri ubwo butumwa yatangaje ku wa mbere, Kainerugaba yagize ati: "Ntidushigikiye abacangero b'abazungu muri DRC. Ntitwigeze tubashigikira. Turashigikiye ko FRN ifata Walikale. UPDF [igisirikare ca Uganda] ntizoyibuza".

FRN ni ihuriro rishasha rya politike na gisirikare rikorera mu buseruko bwa RDC, riherutse kwiyemeza kurwanya ubutegetsi bwa Kinshasa. Rirongowe na Joseph Kabila yahoze arongoye ico gihugu.

Ubutumwa buriko butera impari, Gen Muhoozi yabushize kuri X inyuma y'amakuru yavuga ko hari indege y'intambara y'igisirikare ca RDC yoba yari yakorowe n'abarwanyi, mu bari bayirimwo bikavugwa ko harimwo abacangero b'abazungu.

Reta ya RDC ivuga ko ubwo butumwa buteye impungenge "zikomeye cane" kandi ko bwerekana "ukutubahana kwategerezwa kuba hagati y'ibihugu vyigenga".

Mw'itangazo ubushikiranganji mw'imigenderanire bw'ico gihugu bwashize ahabona ku wa gatatu, bumenyesha ko bwahamagaje ambasaderi wa Uganda i Kinshasa kugira arenguke muri ubwo bushikiranganji.

Mu nama bwagiranye na we, nk'uko iryo tangazo ribandanya ribivuga, bwariyamirije bwivuye inyuma ayo majambo bwongera busaba "insiguro zitomoye" abategetsi ba Uganda.

Mu butumwa bwiwe, Muhoozi yarashimangiye ko ari ngombwa ko Walikale ifatwa. Yagize ati: "Hamwe FRN yoteba, tuzokwifatira Walikale twebwe ubwacu".

Yabandanije ati: "Nta nyungu mfise mu vy'amabuye y'agaciro canke mu kindi kintu ico ari co cose kiri i Walikale. Ico nshaka gusa ni ukurwanya ADF no gukingira umutekano w'abantu banje… Abahema."

Nk'uko bigaragara mw'itangazo ry'ubushikiranganji bw'imigenderanire bwa RDC, Kinshasa ivuga ko irindiriye ko Uganda "isigura icese aho ihagaze" kuri ayo majamabo, ikongera kandi "igafata ingingo zo gukinga ko ibintu nk'ivyo bisubira".

RDC ivuga ko yiyemeje kubungabunga amahoro n'umutekano mu karere, ariko kandi ko itegerezwa kurwanya ico cose coza gihungabanya canke kivogera icubahiro n'ubwigenge bwayo.

Si ubwa mbere Gen Muhoozi atangaje ubutumwa bugateza impari hagati y'ibi bihugu vyompi.

Muri Kigarama (12) mu mwaka wa 2024, RDC na ho nyene yari yahamagaje uwari ahagarariye vy'agateganyo ambasaderi wa Uganda muri ico gihugu imusaba ibisobanuro ku majambo yari yatangajwe na Gen Muhoozi.

MN202611_16olcykkqo.t:
Jersey Mike's signed a five-year sponsorship deal with the EFL in September

Holders Luton Town will host Crystal Palace Under-21s in the last 32 of the Jersey Mike's Trophy.

The Hatters, who beat Stockport County 3-1 in last season's EFL Trophy final at Wembley, won their group in the opening stages of the competition, coming through their three matches unbeaten.

Three-time winners Peterborough United have been drawn away at Plymouth Argyle with Posh hoping to win the trophy for a record fourth time.

Wycombe Wanderers have been handed a potentially attractive tie at home to Arsenal's U21s while Leicester City visit Barnet.

In the northern section, last year's runners-up Stockport will face League Two strugglers Port Vale while Wigan Athletic and Doncaster Rovers, who have both won the competition twice will meet at The Brick Community Stadium.

Managerless Blackpool, who have also won the trophy on two previous occasions have been drawn away at Notts County.

MN202611_pi4cvjx9cd.t:
The strike caused extensive damage to the Abu al-Ouf family's apartment

An Israeli air strike in the Gaza Strip has killed a senior Hamas security official and three members of his family, according to local doctors and the Hamas-run interior ministry.

Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters died when their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City was bombed at dawn, the ministry said.

The Israeli military said Abu al-Ouf was a "terrorist" and that he was eliminated "to remove the threat he posed".

On Tuesday, the overall commander of Hamas's internal security service was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes.

Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza

Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says

Wednesday's strike in Shati caused extensive damage to the Abu al-Ouf family's apartment.

Photos showed the exterior wall and several interior walls were destroyed, with rubble and broken furniture left scattered across the floor.

An interior ministry statement said that Abu al-Ouf was killed along with his wife Noura, 41, and their daughters Yusra, 15, and Jana, 13.

It condemned the attack as a "heinous crime" and accused Israel of targeting security personnel in Gaza "in an effort to spread chaos within Palestinian society".

Hamas's internal security service is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting the group's infrastructure and rooting out informants.

Israel's military said in a statement that Abu al-Ouf was a "significant figure" who had served as "a key source of expertise" in efforts to restrict Israeli counter-terrorism operations in Gaza.

"His elimination is a blow to the apparatus's leadership capabilities and follows yesterday's elimination of his commander," it added.

On Tuesday, an Israeli drone strike in western Gaza City killed Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service.

He had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid in Gaza City by Israeli special forces.

Near daily Israeli strikes continue in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreed in October last year.

At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

MN202611_1kwn0ikfwze.t:
Mahdi Tunsi appears by videolink in front of his attorney Nasser Odeh during his hearing at the Jerusalem District Court on Tuesday

Israeli students, activists and academics are calling for the release of a Palestinian undergraduate who was taken from his university dormitory by Israeli police earlier this month and has since been held without charge.

Mahdi Tunsi, a 26-year-old sociology and criminology student at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, appeared in an Israeli court in the city on Tuesday - a hearing that was held behind closed doors.

Israeli police say he was arrested "concerning ties to an act of terrorism".

Authorities have requested what is known as "administrative detention", which allows the Israeli state to detain people indefinitely without charge on the basis of secret evidence that they cannot see.

"We definitely think this is a political arrest," said Dr Yael Berda, one of Tunsi's university professors.

Tunsi, a Palestinian resident of occupied East Jerusalem who works with well-known Jewish-Palestinian campaign groups, was arrested a month after Israel held an election that saw Arab-led parties win a record 19 seats in parliament, the Knesset, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing coalition lose its majority.

Since then, Berda said she had seen an intensifying campaign against Palestinian rights.

Knesset Member Dr Ofer Cassif was one of the those gathered outside the court

Outside the Jerusalem District Court on Tuesday, demonstrators waved placards with a black-and-white image of Tunsi, while crying out "shame" in unison.

"There's no due process - [administrative detention is] a sugar-coated term for being kidnapped and held as a hostage," said Dr Ofer Cassif, a Member of the Knesset representing the Arab-led Joint List alliance.

"We must all stand firm against such crimes. It's unacceptable."

Since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, which triggered the Gaza war, the number of people in administrative detention has more than doubled .

In October, there were more than 3,100 in administrative detention, according to Israel Prison Service figures published by Israeli rights group HaMoked. Most of them are Palestinians from the occupied West Bank.

Israel says that its use of the policy is compliant with international law and a necessary preventative measure to combat terrorism.

Protesters held signs calling for Tunsi to be freed in Arabic and Hebrew

In a statement, Israeli police said they would "not elaborate further regarding the investigation" into Tunsi.

He appeared via video link from prison - his hair and beard shaved off. His friends also said that he was without medication as well as his glasses, despite a judge requesting them to be brought to him in detention.

The Israel Prison Service said it acted in accordance with the court's rulings.

"When the process was complete and all the necessary approvals had been received, the detainee's lawyer was told he could pass the eyeglasses to the detainee immediately, subject to security procedures," it added.

Berda asked to enter the courtroom on Tuesday but was denied entry. According to Berda, not even Tunsi has been told of the evidence against him.

The judge has said more time is needed to consider the state's request for administrative detention. A decision is expected in the coming days.

The judge has said more time is needed to consider the state's request for administrative detention

"If they have evidence, have them bring it or release him," said Berda.

"That's why we're demanding his immediate release or moving it to a criminal track where he could defend himself."

Berda said that while Tunsi could not vote in Israel's general election because he is not an Israeli citizen, he was "engaged" and very supportive of Arab parties' involvement.

"Mahdi is one of the best human beings I know," said Noga Kaplan, who studies with him at the Hebrew University.

"He has a really pure heart and is very passionate about his studies."

Protesters demand the release of Mahdi Tunsi outside the Jerusalem Central Court during his hearing.

After Tunsi's arrest, the Hebrew University issued a statement saying it was notified a few minutes before it took place.

"The university is not a party to the legal proceedings involving the student, and we do not have information that would allow us to comment on the circumstances leading to the arrest or on the ongoing legal proceedings," it said.

It added that it was concerned for Tunsi's well-being and hoped "that the matter will be resolved promptly and that his rights will be fully respected throughout the process".

Tunsi is a resident of Silwan, a neighbourhood in East Jerusalem where, in recent years, Palestinians have been evicted by Israeli authorities , who say their properties were built illegally. Israeli settlers have since moved into some of those properties.

"Political organisation stopped after October 7 because people were getting super scared about the consequences," explained Kaplan.

"Mahdi saw studying as one of the ways to speak about it in class."

"He didn't do a lot of public stuff because what's happening now is his biggest fear."

MN202611_wrw593o2np.t:
Vincent Harper is on a season-long loan at Exeter City from Walsall

Vincent Harper says he relished the chance to play for Kenya during the international break.

The Exeter City wing-back, on loan from League Two rivals Walsall, came on in his country's 2-1 Africa Cup of Nations qualifier loss to South Africa in Nairobi last week.

It was his second cap this season, having played 90 minutes against Rwanda in a friendly last month.

"It's a massive honour," Harper told BBC Radio Devon.

"My parents were both born there, it just feels almost like you're repaying back, not to them but also to the whole country.

"It's a lot of pressure at the same time, but overall it's just a big honour."

Harper has played 13 times since returning to Exeter this season - he had a two-year spell at St James Park before he joined Walsall in the summer of 2025.

The former Bristol City youth player made his English Football League debut when he moved to Exeter from Eastleigh in 2023 and went on to play 65 times in all competitions before moving to the Midlands.

"I think it just shows you the next level or the level you need to be at to play consistently at an international level," he added.

"It's very intense and very quick and you're playing with the best of the best of the country so you've got to definitely be at your 'A' game.

"If you make one mistake then you'll definitely be punished."

Exeter City bring in Harper and Samuel on loan

Harper started all seven of Exeter's games after arriving back at the club.

But while he was away on international duty in October, Exeter hit a rich vein of form and he has not been able to get back into the starting line-up.

He is hopeful he can force his way back into a side that has been one of League Two's in-form teams over the past two months - Exeter have risen from close to the relegation zone to the brink of the play-off places after just one loss in their past 10 games in all competitions.

"It's a bit of a frustrating one," he admitted. "Before the first internationals I was heavily involved and then the boys started doing well while I was away.

"It's nice to see the boys doing well, but I want to be more part of it and spend more time on the pitch and show them what I can do.

"But overall it's good to see the team winning and although I might not get as many minutes as I want, it's nice to come on here and there and play my part as well."

MN202611_so4el0wbzm.t:
Nottingham Forest have suffered successive 2-0 defeats on the road to Brentford and Bournemouth

Nottingham Forest manager Oliver Glasner says standards at the club were not good enough when he arrived, and has questioned why some of his squad cannot speak English after being in the country for a number of years.

Forest are one place above the relegation zone heading into Friday's home game against Chelsea , winning just two of their first 11 games in the Premier League.

"Stability in a company is having standards," said Glasner. "Everybody who joins commits to the standards. I think, very honestly, the standards were not high enough.

"We have players who are here for four years, can't speak English. If you go to Italy, after three months, every player gives his interview in the Italian language.

"For me, if I want to manage in England, I have to speak English. If I want to manage in Italy, I have to speak Italian.

"Otherwise, Oliver Glasner, if you want to speak in your dialect, stay at home in Austria, everybody understands you, but nowhere else."

Forest, who narrowly avoided relegation last season but who did reach the Europa League semi-finals, have had a succession of managers in recent years and while Glasner refused to blame the upheaval for any problems he has inherited, he feels standards need to rise.

"We want to create a stable Nottingham Forest team that can consistently play in the top half of the Premier League," added Glasner, 52.

"We are a few steps away from this but we really believe we know which steps we have to take.

"We are still very ambitious but it looks to take a little bit longer than we all hoped. The goal is getting stability into this club and we're still working on this.

"We knew this is a transition season, let's say like this, where we still stay very ambitious but with a lot of problems to solve."

Glasner held transfer talks with Forest owner Evangelos Marinakis in London on Monday as the club prepares their plans for the January transfer window, when they hope to add up to five players to their squad.

"He [Marinakis] was asking 'what do you need, what do you want here to improve in the squad, the staff and the environment'," said Glasner.

"He wants the best for Nottingham Forest , he wants the best for everyone here.

"We need to improve in the squad, in the staff, in the environment and this is our discussion. It was a fantastic meeting and it was worth spending six hours travelling."

MN202611_1tpgd6u99no.t:
The BBC has lodged an "urgent" appeal against a US judge's decision to allow Donald Trump's $10bn (£7.6bn) lawsuit against the corporation to go ahead.

The US president is suing the BBC for defamation over the way an episode of Panorama edited a speech he gave in January 2021, shortly before the riot at the US Capitol.

Earlier this month, a federal judge in Florida ruled that the defamation case could proceed after the BBC sought to dismiss it.

The BBC has now filed an appeal with a higher court, saying there is a "complete lack of evidence" that anyone in Florida accessed the programme, and that the broadcaster made "rigorous and systematic efforts to prevent access to the documentary" in the US.

A BBC spokesman said: "We are surprised and disappointed by the court's decision that this case should be heard in Florida.

"As we have made clear from the start, the BBC broadcast this documentary in the UK - and UK only. We did not show it in Florida, nor did any other broadcaster.

"Given the urgency of this issue, we are now requesting a higher court review the ruling."

President Trump's lawsuit accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave on 6 January 2021.

The BBC has apologised for the edit in Trump: A Second Chance, which it said had given "the mistaken impression that President Trump made a direct call for violent action".

But the corporation argued that the Panorama episode, which was broadcast in 2024, did not meet the legal criteria for defamation.

Earlier this month, federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz found Trump's defamation allegations against the BBC sufficient for the case to continue, although he did not rule on the merits of the case.

President Trump called the judge's ruling a "huge victory" in a post on Truth Social at the time.

The BBC has now lodged an appeal with the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, arguing that the Florida court has no jurisdiction to hear the case.

Trump has been ordered to answer questions under oath as part of the lawsuit by 22 January.

Judge Kuntz has scheduled a trial date for the case for 3 May 2027 in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.

Judge allows Trump's $10bn defamation case against BBC to proceed

MN202611_1edit6sbpnm.t:
Donald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times this year, a review of the US president's financial disclosures shows.

Trump's most recent public declarations of his investment trading show that between January and September the portfolios purchased between $5.2m and $17m (£4m and £13m) in Nvidia stock - and sold between $4.4m and $12m. His portfolios held between $12.5m and $58m of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025.

Financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics report a low and high range of transaction values, so a more precise analysis of how much Nvidia stock was traded is not possible.

The period of recent turmoil at Nvidia and volatility in its share price is not covered by the disclosures. In the last two weeks, co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang resigned and then Trump played a significant part in his reinstatement.

The White House has said that Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties and neither he nor his family "has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold".

Huang resigned on 12 November after reports of extramarital affairs, including with one woman who has alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's share price dived following news of his resignation.

But on Monday Nvidia's board announced the 63-year-old was being reinstated as CEO.

Trump told US media he had "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring Huang back. The board said it had "received input from senior levels of the United States government" that he posed "no national security risk".

Nvidia's share price surged 31% on Monday following Huang's return. About $1tn (£763bn) was added to Nvidia's market value, but the company's shares are still trading below their value before reports of Huang's alleged affairs began to circulate.

However, concerns remain among both Republican and Democratic politicians about Huang's actions and Nvidia's compliance with US controls over the export of advanced computer chips to China, as well as Trump's involvement in getting him reappointed as CEO.

Nvidia's chip technology and investments have been critical to the growth of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry , leading to it becoming one of the world's most valuable companies.

The firm now represents more than 6% of the S&P 500 share index, according to State Street financial services. This makes it the second most valuable company on the index after Apple, whose shares Trump's accounts also frequently trade.

Nvidia also ranks highly in many global indices, meaning that investment accounts held around the world, including pensions, are likely to include its shares.

Our analysis of Trump's Nvidia trades does not include other investment products held by him which may include its shares.

Trump made at least $2.2bn (£1.7bn) from a variety of investments and commercial activities, according to the financial disclosure report for the first year of Trump's second term.

Barbara Perry, a presidential historian at the University of Virginia's Miller Center, told the BBC there is "no precedent for this," adding: "It's beyond anything we've ever seen in the presidency."

MN202611_1l3cgpj5d6d.t:
Smoke appears after explosion heard in Iowa near Army detonation site

The US military has hailed as a "huge success" the detonation of nearly five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa, an operation that sparked widespread fears of health and environmental problems across the region.

Smoke was seen rising into the sky shortly after 09:00 local time (14:00 GMT) following the explosion, as the army declared the risk "as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible".

President Donald Trump said reports showed the mitigation efforts "far exceeded expectations".

Plans to detonate the lead azide, a highly volatile compound reportedly at risk of exploding on its own, were paused multiple times before Wednesday's detonation following public outcry and legal challenges.

Despite widespread concern from residents of Middletown, Iowa ahead of the blast, officials have said that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.

"The Army's controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success," Adam Telle, acting secretary of the US Army, wrote on social media.

"We are watching EPA's [Environmental Protection Agency] MASSIVE sensor array throughout the area closely, and there are no readings so far above 0.0," he added.

The explosives had been in storage for around 20 years, and degraded as part of a process known as recrystallisation - this made them more responsive to accidental detonation from friction or other movement.

No level of lead exposure is considered safe, with children and pregnant women particularly vulnerable to its harmful effects.

Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson told the BBC he felt "relieved" and "vindicated" after the detonation.

He watched the blast from his job at a manufacturing plant eight miles (12km) away from the blast - and monitored a camera at his two-bedroom home just one mile from the detonation site.

"We did not feel anything. We did not see anything," Johnson said.

Some eight miles (12km) away from Middletown, Sandy Mabeus closed the windows and the garage at her home, brought their outdoor cat inside and hunkered down earlier today.

The family watched three separate live streams on iPads and televisions of the explosion as it happened.

"We did not feel or hear a thing here," she told the BBC, adding that she checked the videos to confirm it had actually happened.

"The waiting and wondering has not been a good thing for anybody in the area," she said. "Hopefully they had a very good result and we can just get on with things."

There is also caution from some quarters.

Iowa's incoming Governor-elect Rob Sand said there was "more testing to do" and called for "immediate transparency" to explain why the lead-up was "so chaotic and unclear".

Sand said that any Iowans who have been impacted in any way "must be taken care of fully, right away".

Cameron Hamilton, administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), said there would be additional resources and testing in the coming days and weeks.

In recent weeks, the army scheduled and rescheduled their detonation ahead of colder winter temperatures.

It also warned locals of "potential exposure to toxic lead dust", which led to some panic. They instituted measures including an optional evacuation zone and a shelter-in-place advisory ahead of the detonation.

The army faced pushback from residents and politicians alike and there were legal challenges to prevent the detonation from going ahead on environmental and health grounds.

But on Monday, the appeals court overturned a decision to halt the blast. It said that - while these concerns were valid - the risk from an unplanned explosion was greater.

Sheila Flynn and Kwasi Gyamfi Asiedu contributed to this report

MN202611_9l3j59wfm3.t:
Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang

North Korea has ordered Switzerland's diplomatic representative to leave the country within 48 hours and called for the office to close amid a row over sanctions.

It said the move was in response to Switzerland's decision to place sanctions on the Songdowon international children's camp. State media described this as "a blatant hostile act".

That camp is at the centre of claims that it was involved in transferring children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.

North Korea's foreign ministry said "any act of violating the sovereign rights" of the country and the interests of its citizens "can never be welcomed".

Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang.

Swiss authorities said relations between the two countries would be maintained through the North Korean embassy in Bern, and the Swiss embassy in Beijing.

The diplomatic rebuke comes weeks after Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis made a rare visit to North Korea, where he officially reopened the office and discussed normalising relations.

Diplomatic links with North Korea were first established in 1974 and Switzerland opened a co-operation office in Pyongyang in 1997.

A Swiss delegation, on left, including Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis, met with North Korean officials in Pyongyang last month

Switzerland's federal department of foreign affairs said the country "distinguishes between its sanctions policy and its commitment to maintaining dialogue with all countries".

It added: "The reopening of the office in Pyongyang did not in any way affect Switzerland's implementation of UN sanctions related to North Korea's nuclear programme, nor its implementation of EU sanctions targeting North Korea in the context of Russia's war against Ukraine."

Thousands of North Korean soldiers have been deployed to help support Russia's war with Ukraine.

In August, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of using North Korean missiles.

The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface.

Video released by Nasa showed the moment of impact in 2022, while new images show the extent of the damage done to the asteroid.

Dimorphos, the asteroid, posed no threat to Earth, but the crash was a test of our planetary defences to see if it was possible to knock a space rock off course.

Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision.

The BBC's science editor Rebecca Morelle explains.

MN202611_yll989mfvb.t:
KIGALI – Homepoint Rwanda has officially launched global home appliance brand Haier in Rwanda, marking a major milestone for the company and bringing an extensive range of innovative home appliances, HVAC solutions, water heating technologies and smart home solutions to the Rwandan market.

The grand launch, held at the Kigali Marriott Hotel, brought together business clients, dealers, wholesalers, property developers and other key stakeholders to celebrate the strategic partnership between Homepoint and Haier, with Homepoint appointed as Haier’s Country Distributor in Rwanda.

The event was attended by senior Haier representatives, including Yang Dong Qi, Regional Manager for Haier East Africa, and Yang Shuai, Marketing Director for Haier Middle East and Africa (MEA), who highlighted the brand’s global strength, technological innovation and ambitions for the African market.

Haier, recognized as the world’s No. 1 major home appliance brand for 17 consecutive years, offers an extensive portfolio of products ranging from refrigerators, washing machines, televisions, air conditioners, freezers and cookers to built-in kitchen appliances, water heaters, solar water heating systems and smart home technologies.

The introduction of Haier is expected to further strengthen Rwanda’s appliance market by offering consumers and businesses access to international technology, energy-efficient products, intelligent solutions and a wider choice of premium appliances.

Haier’s Global Strength and African Commitment

Yang Dong Qi, highlighted the company’s commitment to building sustainable business capabilities across Africa, rather than simply supplying products to the continent.

“One of the most important things Haier has done in Africa over the past few years is not shipping products. It is building capability,” he said.

He explained that the partnership brings together Haier’s global technology, brand strength and systems with Homepoint’s local market knowledge, customer relationships and retail network.

“For Rwanda, this means that supply is not coming from a single point. Regional capacity can support local delivery, while our research and development capabilities help us respond to different power, climate and housing conditions,” he said.

Yang added that Haier continues to strengthen its marketing, logistics, digitalization and after-sales service networks to deliver an improved customer experience across the region.

Haier’s global footprint includes operations in more than 200 countries and regions, over 10 research and development centers, 35 industrial parks, 143 manufacturing centers and 126 marketing centers. Its products and services reach more than one billion households worldwide.

Homepoint: 16 Years of Innovation and Growth

Addressing the gathering, Manoj Skariah, Managing Director of Homepoint Rwanda, described the launch as a significant milestone in the company’s 16-year journey in Rwanda.

Homepoint is the trade name of Hotpoint Appliances Rwanda Ltd., and the Homepoint brand was unveiled in 2024.

He highlighted Homepoint’s longstanding commitment to introducing international brands, innovative business models and technologies that enhance the consumer experience and contribute to the development of Rwanda’s retail and appliance industry.

“Over the last 16 years, Homepoint has always believed in leading the industry through strategy, innovation and bringing the best brands and technologies to Rwanda,” he said.

He explained that Homepoint has continuously evolved, introduced new ideas and created opportunities for our customers. Today, partnering with Haier, the world’s No. 1 major appliance brand, is another important chapter in that journey.

In his address, Murli Menon, CEO of Homepoint, emphasized that Haier’s arrival represents more than the introduction of a new brand.

“It has a broad product range, advanced technology, energy efficiency and smart features offer solutions for households, commercial customers, hospitality establishments and property developers,” he said.

Menon noted that the brand’s extensive portfolio, including HVAC, solar water heating and smart home automation, positions it to serve Rwanda’s growing demand for modern homes, commercial buildings and integrated living solutions.

Innovation Beyond Products and Partnering with Flexipay Microfinance

Manoj also highlighted Homepoint’s track record of introducing innovative consumer financing solutions to make quality products more accessible.

The company was among the pioneers of the Buy Now, Pay Later concept in Rwanda’s consumer appliance sector through its partnership with I&M Bank under the Ryoshya Iwawe initiative, enabling eligible bank customers to acquire appliances and pay in instalments.

Building on this experience, Homepoint is now expanding access to consumer financing through its new partnership with FlexiPay, a microfinance institution, allowing a broader range of consumers to access flexible payment solutions irrespective of their banking relationship.

“This is how we believe innovation should work. It should not only introduce new technology and products, but also find better ways for our customers to access them. We want quality, innovation and modern living to become more accessible to Rwandan consumers,” he said.

A New Chapter for Rwanda’s Appliance Market

The Haier launch reinforces Homepoint’s commitment to bringing leading international brands and innovative solutions to Rwanda.

With an established distribution network, showrooms, warehousing facilities and after-sales service capabilities, Homepoint is positioned to support the brand’s growth and ensure customers have access to products, technical support and reliable service.

The partnership is expected to create new opportunities for dealers, wholesalers, developers, hospitality operators and other business partners while contributing to the continued modernization of Rwanda’s home appliance and home solutions market.

As Haier enters Rwanda through Homepoint, the partnership signals a shared ambition to make homes smarter, more comfortable, energy-efficient and connected.

For more information, visit www.homepoint.rw .

MN202611_ezn0v5mb1.t:
KIGALI – More than 840 enterprises have been reached through a nationwide campaign to introduce businesses to Rwanda’s capital markets, as the country seeks to expand the sources of long-term financing available to private companies and mobilize more domestic investment.

The campaign comes at a time when many businesses still face basic challenges that make it difficult for companies to demonstrate their financial performance and convince investors to commit capital.

The second edition of the Capital Markets Roadshows, organized by the Capital Markets Authority (CMA) in partnership with other partners concluded in Kigali on Wednesday, November 25, after engagements across the country’s provinces.

The campaign aimed at bringing businesses closer to financing options beyond conventional bank lending, particularly equity and corporate bonds, which can support expansion, new projects and longer-term investment.

CMA Chief Executive Officer Romeo Ngarambe.

CMA Chief Executive Officer Romeo Ngarambe said the roadshows had demonstrated interest among businesses, but stressed that the next step was to turn that interest into actual capital mobilization.

“Bank lending remains essential, and it will continue to be. But it cannot meet every financial need, and long-term projects need long-term financing or long-term money,” he said.

Through equity financing, a company can bring investors on board by selling shares, while corporate bonds allow businesses to borrow directly from investors without surrendering ownership.

Ngarambe said some business owners hesitate to sell shares because they fear losing control, yet companies can raise capital by offering minority stakes while retaining decision-making authority.

He also encouraged businesses to seek advice from licensed market professionals to identify financing structures suited to their needs.

Preparing Businesses to Attract Investment

For enterprises seeking capital, however, access to investors is only part of the equation. Businesses must demonstrate that they have reliable financial records, sound governance, credible plans and a clear purpose for the money they intend to raise.

Clement Uwajeneza, the Chief Executive Officer of PSF, said the lack of regular financial records among businesses remains a significant obstacle to accessing investment.

He cited the 2023 establishment census, which found that about four in ten businesses did not maintain regular accounts, and said investors also need to understand how companies make decisions and plan for growth.

“An investor is also looking and wanting to understand who makes the decision in the business. That’s proper governance. Where it plans to be in the three to five years to come, and how the money it raises is going to help it get there,” Uwajeneza said.

He said the roadshows should encourage business owners to examine their bookkeeping, management structures and growth plans, adding that PSF would continue supporting enterprises with financial planning, governance and investment proposals.

“If a business goes home and starts working on even one of those things, this initiative has already been a success,” he said.

The drive to expand capital market participation is also linked to Rwanda’s wider development and investment targets.

Herbert Asiimwe, Head of Financial Sector Development at the Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning, said the second National Strategy for Transformation (NST2) targets annual economic growth of at least nine per cent and more than 250,000 non-agricultural jobs each year.

Achieving those targets will require substantial long-term investment, he said, with domestic savings playing a greater role alongside foreign capital.

The government is targeting national savings equivalent to about 26 per cent of GDP, with capital markets expected to help mobilize those resources and direct them towards productive activities.

Asiimwe said the government also wants to make investment products more accessible to ordinary citizens, including through digital platforms that would allow people to buy shares and other securities without travelling to Kigali.

He urged financial institutions and regulators to make market procedures easier to understand, while encouraging citizens to consider investment opportunities beyond traditional banking products.

“Life does not start and end with the banks, MFIs or Umurenge SACCOs. There’s a very big opportunity for us on the capital markets,” he said.

The government also wants to see a wider range of financing instruments, including municipal bonds that could allow local authorities to raise funds for infrastructure such as hospitals, schools and stadiums.

The longer-term objective is to see more businesses become investment-ready, more citizens participate as investors and more capital flow into enterprises capable of expanding production and creating jobs.

Some 12.3 million people watched the show's hotly anticipated cliffhanger finale on Christmas Day in 2024

Fans of Gavin and Stacey will be given the chance to get their hands on "really cool, one-off pieces of memorabilia" from the filming of the much-loved TV show's 2024 finale.

Items include the West Ham football shirts worn by James Corden, Rob Brydon and Mathew Horne at Smithy's stag do and a clapperboard signed by the cast of the BBC sitcom.

Some 12.3 million people watched the show's hotly anticipated cliffhanger finale on Christmas Day in 2024.

The memorabilia has been donated by Tidy Productions, one of the companies behind the show, to raise money for Cancer Research Wales - with the online auction beginning on Wednesday.

Smithy's West Ham football shirt worn by James Corden is one of the items available at auction

Adam Fletcher, chief executive of Welsh Cancer Research, said: "We're extremely lucky to have these items donated."

Speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast , Fletcher said the money raised by the sale would help "fund new cancer research in Wales".

"All the money stays in Wales," he said.

"I think it's really nice that probably the biggest TV programme ever to come out of Wales has come to support us."

The auction is set to close on 14 December.

A clapperboard from the final scene signed by cast members, including Ruth Jones, James Corden, Joanna Page, Rob Brydon and Mathew Horne

The sale of the items has been supported by the show's co-creators and stars, Ruth Jones and James Corden.

Other items available at auction include two paintings that were hung on the wall of Gwen's house, an official "finale production" crew hoodie and a range of DVDs.

Aside from the DVDs, the charity confirmed all items will be accompanied by a letter of authenticity from Tidy Productions.

French military combat engineering experts are in Rwanda to help the Rwanda Defence Force (RDF) develop specialised capabilities to detect, prevent and respond to improvised explosive devices (IEDs), commonly known as homemade bombs.

The French team, led by Lt Col Benoît Saint-Paul and accompanied by France’s Defence Attaché to Rwanda, Col Cyril Chevauchet, visited the RDF Engineer Command Headquarters, where they were received by the Deputy Commander, Col Marie Claire Muragijimana.

The visit is aimed at strengthening military cooperation between France and Rwanda through the exchange of technical knowledge and expertise, with a particular focus on developing a specialised Counter-Improvised Explosive Devices (C-IED) capability.

IEDs are explosives made or assembled using materials that are not necessarily designed for military use. They can be concealed along roads, inside buildings or in other locations before being detonated remotely or through contact.

They are frequently used in conflicts involving armed groups, particularly in areas where conventional military forces face irregular warfare tactics. Roadside bombs, for instance, have caused significant casualties among soldiers and civilians in conflict zones across Africa and elsewhere.

Counter-IED operations involve identifying explosive threats, detecting devices, safely dealing with them and disrupting the networks responsible for making and deploying them.

For the RDF, developing this capability could strengthen the protection of troops operating in areas affected by armed conflict, including during peacekeeping missions and other security operations.

Combat engineers play an important role in military operations, supporting troop movements, clearing obstacles, constructing defensive positions and dealing with explosive hazards.

The French engagement is expected to contribute to RDF’s technical expertise in this specialised field, although details of the proposed training, equipment support and implementation arrangements were not disclosed.

The visit comes amid continued security challenges in several African conflict zones, where improvised explosive devices have increasingly been used by armed groups against military forces and civilians.

MN202611_w2a30t2zhn.t:
Benjamin Netanyahu called for his trial to be ended "immediately"

Judges in Israel have suggested prosecutors drop bribery charges against Benjamin Netanyahu, potentially handing the caretaker prime minister a boost as he fights for his political survival.

The judges told the attorney general that there was little chance of conviction in the first of three cases he is facing, in which he is accused of granting government favours in exchange for positive media coverage.

They also questioned whether his actions amounted to criminal conduct in a second corruption case, and suggested prosecutors seek a plea deal in a third.

Netanyahu has consistently denied the allegations against him and called on Wednesday for the trial to be ended "immediately".

"Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family, my son," he said in a televised statement.

"Ten years of incitement to hatred that wounds the soul."

Netanyahu was first charged in 2019, but court proceedings have been prolonged in part by the recent Israel-Gaza war.

The case now under serious doubt, known as Case 4,000, concerns an alleged "reciprocal arrangement" between Netanyahu and the controlling shareholder in Israel's biggest telecoms company. Both denied any wrongdoing.

In a highly unusual step, a judging panel at the Jerusalem District Court summoned Israeli Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara on Wednesday to express their concerns.

"The chances of conviction are low – to an extent that warrants reconsidering the matter," Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman told her, Israeli media reported.

The judges also cast doubt on whether Netanyahu's actions, which are subject to a second case – concerning another alleged quid-pro-quo with another media baron, known as Case 2,000 – met the threshold for criminality.

While they left open the possibility of a conviction in the third case: Case 1,000, which alleges Netanyahu acted for the benefit of an Australian billionaire after being gifted cigars and champagne by him.

Netanyahu: What are the corruption charges?

However, the judges told the attorney general that, in the public interest, there needed to be a "rethink" in how the trial should move forward, Israeli media report.

Baharav-Miara said she would consider the judges' recommendations.

It has been six years since Netanyahu became Israel's first sitting prime minister to face a criminal trial.

He has always claimed to be the victim of a political witch-hunt and said on Wednesday that the "fabricated cases" against him were now falling apart.

The cases have continued to progress in court while Netanyahu remained in power throughout the war in Gaza, though judges agreed to reduce the number of hearings due to security concerns around the conflict.

The accusations against him have rocked Israeli politics, fuelling already deep divisions. His trial has coincided with controversial, far-reaching judiciary reforms by Netanyahu's government.

For his opponents, Netanyahu's fear of prison has distorted his decision-making as prime minister and made him especially dependent on his far-right coalition partners to remain in power.

This latest development will give a boost to Netanyahu, whose political opponent Gadi Eisenkot is currently attempting to form a coalition government after an inconclusive general election last month.

While Netanyahu's parliamentary bloc won more seats than that of his rival, both fell short of an outright majority. Israel's president has offered Eisenkot the first chance to form a new administration.

Netanyahu remains subject to an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, which he also denies.

MN202611_1fejg4abdiw.t:
Manchester City are currently third in the Premier League

The chair of English football's independent regulator has told MPs he "has the stomach" to take potential action against Manchester City .

The club was found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules over a nine-season period by an independent commission.

The verdict, published in September, found City's Abu Dhabi owners - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president Sheikh Mansour - inflated revenues and disguised losses by £900 million through "sham" arrangements.

City deny wronging and have appealed, but if the ruling is upheld, they could face an investigation by the Independent Football Regulator (IFR).

It has the power to remove directors if they are deemed unsuitable, and even to force a sale of the club.

Appearing in front of parliament's Digital, Culture, Media and Sport select committee, IFR chairman David Kogan was clear that the watchdog would not be afraid to investigate the club's hierarchy and take action, if deemed necessary.

"Forget the name of the club, forget the size of the club, forget the scale of the issue. We cannot simply ignore our statutory duties in relation to a club because it happens to be of a certain size," he said.

"We absolutely will have to take the appropriate action as laid out in the legislation, depending on the circumstances as they come to us, which are the evidence that's been presented and collated by the independent commission of the Premier League and by any judgement that takes place on that evidence through an appeal.

"But in one sense, the evidence has already been judged by those cases having been found guilty, so we will absolutely have the stomach to do so.

"Would I, with an organisation that has a relatively new, fairly young staff, that's been going for less than a year, would I have chosen to have this particular issue in our laps this early? Well, probably not.

"But the truth is, if we don't act - assuming those circumstances are triggered - if we don't act, what is the purpose of having a football regulator?

"So I think we have to absolutely, clearly be seen to be doing the job that you as legislators have asked us to do, and we absolutely will do that, whatever that means."

De Bruyne's feelings for Man City will 'never change'

Premier League clubs to cover legal costs if Man City sponsors sue

The fallout from the case has prompted concern that wider UAE investment in UK projects could suffer. In September, Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" if the scandal led to City's owners selling the club.

Kogan added: "Does the evidence, if we come to assess it in relation to individuals, stand up in terms of the legislation as being a cause for concern? And if it is, we will have to act appropriately.

"That is the only test, not the politics around it, not the place where it came from, not the size of the club. It is the only test because without that, you cannot have an effective regulator."

When asked how any possible legal battles with City would be paid for, IFR chief executive Richard Monks said a litigation reserve of £2m was to be built up over the next two years via a levy charged to the clubs. "When we take litigation, we expect to win and we expect to reclaim costs and repay that reserve from costs," he said.

"Now clearly - and I'm not talking about a specific case - clearly, there could be a very large legal case of any particular club that would require us to spend more than £2m in terms of litigation costs and barrister costs in particular. So if that happens, we have agreed with government [that it] will effectively lend us the money in terms of cash flow.

"As I say, we'd expect to win that litigation, to claim costs and repay government. If we failed in that massive litigation, then ultimately it would be added to the levy and we'd repay government that way."

MN202611_1vtnritgnzn.t:
Huge fire erupts near Cairo killing at least 30 people

At least 30 people have been killed and 19 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.

Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and smoke inhalation after the incident, which occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, to the north of the old city centre, on Wednesday evening.

Unverified footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.

Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported the fuel truck had overturned, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.

The regional public prosecutor has launched an investigation into the incident and asked that DNA samples be taken from bodies of the dead.

The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, had been travelling along the highway when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, prompting the driver to lose control, Al-Ahram reports, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation.

It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the state-owned newspaper says.

Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, with informal residential areas and often run-down infrastructure making incidents more common, the response to which is often complicated by slow emergency response times and locally improvised rescue efforts, even in the sprawling Egyptian capital.

Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished, as emergency services blocked off entry routes.

Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished

The tanker crossed the highway's central reservation before overturning and bursting into flames, local media report

The health ministry said 39 ambulances had been dispatched to respond to the fire, while it posted images of Egypt's health minister overseeing the treatment of the injured at one of Cairo's hospitals.

Road collisions are also common in Egypt, often attributed to lax maintenance and the widespread flouting of traffic laws.

Nearly 6,000 people died on Egypt's roads last year, official figures show, a rise of several hundred on the previous year's total.

Emergency responders have since cleared the highway and allowed it to reopen, state broadcaster NMA reports.

A bulldozer could earlier be seen at the scene clearing the burnt-out wrecks of cars.

MN202611_fu3nkawk14.t:
Andy Taylor's guitar riffs powered some of Duran Duran's best-known songs

Andy Taylor, the guitarist for the pop group Duran Duran, has died at the age of 65.

Born in Tynemouth, he co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits, including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film; and also worked with artists like Robert Palmer, Rod Stewart and Belinda Carlisle.

In a statement, his bandmates said Taylor had fought "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer" and "passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23 November".

His wife, Tracey, said the musician "was the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day".

The son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.

He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran.

The group went on to achieve global fame through the New Romantic movement, which combined slick, melodic synth-pop with aspirational music videos and chiselled good looks.

Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.

"Andy was there at the very beginning of our story," said his bandmates Simon LeBon, Nick Rhodes, John Taylor and Roger Taylor (his bandmates were unrelated, despite sharing the same last name).

"From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.

"Our thoughts are with his wife Tracey, his children Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew, and grandson Albie. They all loved him deeply and we ask that their privacy be respected at this very difficult time."

MN202611_yfiibgafq2.t:
Ferguson was named as Glentoran boss in October

If Duncan Ferguson is to be a success at Glentoran, it will be without the benefit of any new manager bounce.

The former Everton striker arrived at the Oval in October amid plenty of fanfare and sparked hopes that the high-profile left-field appointment would be the one to lead the Glens to a first Irish Premiership title since 2009.

However, under the Scot the east Belfast outfit have struggled for results, registering just one win in five matches, and exited the BetMcLean Cup after being beaten at home by Larne on Tuesday night.

On top of their inconsistent form, Ferguson was handed a seven-game suspension following a red card for arguing with officials in the side's 3-2 defeat by Cliftonville last week and will not be back in the dugout until 2027.

Ferguson was sent off at Solitude and has since apologised

Earning his first Irish Premiership red card in just his fourth match in charge was an unwanted milestone for Ferguson but it is the resulting suspension that poses a more significant problem.

The 1995 FA Cup winner was dismissed for the way he addressed match officials after believing the Reds' opener at Solitude should have been ruled out for a foul in the build-up.

Ferguson has since apologised but will now miss a string of key games including the highly anticipated 'Big Two' Boxing Day derby, a match that may not require much of a team talk from the manager but is perhaps biggest single fixture in the Irish Premiership calendar.

While Ferguson must watch his new team from the stands, assistant coach Gary Bollan will take charge with the help of goalkeeping coach Elliot Morris.

"Yeah, I think it's a big miss for us in the changing room, not having his voice and not having his persona in the changing room," Morris said when asked about Ferguson's ban.

"He's a big character, but it is what it is and we'll just have to accept it and get on with it.

"He's accepted it, the club's accepted it, we'll just get on with it and try and focus for the second Larne match."

Following Declan Devine's departure in September, results under interim manager Paddy McCourt and coach Tim McCann suggested that the Glens may be beginning to turn a corner, but Ferguson has so far found it difficult to build upon that progress.

Five points from four games in the Irish Premiership, now paired with the setback of a cup exit, shows that there is plenty for Ferguson to address.

Victory over Bangor remains the highlight of the new manager's tenure to date, but even that win was only secured thanks to Cal Weatherup's 87th-minute winner.

Indeed, the upturn in form of striker Weatherup has been one bright point for the side in recent weeks.

After limited minutes at the start of the season, the 18-year-old has now netted three goals in his past three games.

His emergence is particularly welcome given leading striker Pat Hoban continues to work his way back from injury and former Northern Ireland international Conor McMenamin looks to recapture his best form after returning to the Irish Premiership in the summer.

Ferguson will know the importance of the Glens looking like more of a threat in the final third and one of his aims will be to help the former Glentoran academy forward continue his recent form and bolster the east Belfast side's front-line.

Ferguson made 123 appearances for Everton

Ferguson will surely have already seen enough to start on his plans to help the Glens end their long wait for Premiership success - even if he is to be watching the next six games from a frustrating remove.

His personality and contacts are still to be major assets for the Glens and he can continue to put his stamp on the side during training.

Ferguson has already signed one player during his time at the club - free agent Nathan Shaw - but the January transfer window will give him the opportunity to bring in further fresh faces.

The Glens sit in fourth and 17 points behind league leaders Linfield in the Premiership, but there will be another chance to seal silverware in the form of the Irish Cup, a competition they have won 23 times.

By the time Glentoran come into that competition in January, Ferguson will finally be back in dugout rather than the director's box.

Ferguson's tenure will not be defined by these early days, but he is experienced enough to know that a quick upturn in results is crucial.

For now, all attention turns to Friday's Irish Premiership rematch against the Inver Reds - live on BBC iPlayer - as Ferguson's side look to get their season back on track without him on the sidelines.
